posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params, Not Compute
posts.subtitle: How trillion-parameter models keep inference cheap: only wake up a few experts per token.
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces a dense feed-forward layer with many smaller 'expert' feed-forward networks plus a router that activates only a few per token. This decouples total parameter count from per-token compute, letting models like Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 pack hundreds of billions of parameters while only running a fraction of them on any given token.

slides.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params, Not Compute
slides.body: In a dense transformer, every parameter runs on every token. MoE breaks that link: a router picks a handful of 'expert' sub-networks per token, so total capacity can grow far faster than per-token compute.
bullets: Swap one big feed-forward layer for many small expert feed-forward layers
A learned router sends each token to only a few experts (commonly 1-2 of 8, or 8 of 256)
Total parameters can be 5-10x higher than active parameters per token

slides.title: Dense scaling makes compute and parameters grow together
slides.body: In a standard dense model, doubling the parameter count roughly doubles the FLOPs needed per token, because every weight participates in every forward pass. That coupling makes trillion-parameter dense models prohibitively expensive to train and serve.
bullets: FLOPs per token in a dense FFN scale directly with hidden size and parameter count
More capacity (knowledge, specialization) has historically meant strictly more compute per request
Serving cost and latency rise in lockstep with model size — there's no lever to pull separately

slides.title: A router decides which experts see each token
slides.body: Each MoE layer has N expert FFNs and a small gating network. For every token, the gate scores all experts, picks the top-k (often k=1 or k=2), and combines their outputs weighted by the gate's softmax scores.
bullets: Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing, 46.7B total params but only ~12.9B active per forward pass
DeepSeek-V3: 671B total params, but only ~37B active per token thanks to fine-grained expert routing
Unselected experts don't run at all for that token — their weights sit idle, costing memory but not compute

slides.title: Keeping the router honest: load balancing
slides.body: Left alone, a router tends to collapse onto a few favorite experts, starving the rest of training signal (and FLOPs capacity). MoE training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven expert usage.
bullets: Each expert has a fixed 'capacity' (max tokens per batch); overflow tokens get dropped or rerouted, directly hurting quality if misconfigued
Expert-parallel serving shards experts across GPUs and requires an all-to-all communication step to send tokens to their assigned expert's device
Capacity factor and load-balance loss weight are real hyperparameters — too strict balancing can hurt specialization, too loose causes dropped tokens

slides.title: Total params vs. active params
slides.body: The headline MoE number isn't total size — it's how much smaller the active compute is relative to that size.

slides.title: Worked example: one token through a Mixtral layer
slides.body: Take the token 'bank' in the sentence 'I deposited money at the bank.' The gate computes a score for all 8 experts from the token's hidden state, softmaxes them, and keeps only the top 2.
bullets: Say Expert 3 scores 0.55 and Expert 7 scores 0.30 (the rest score lower and are dropped)
The token's hidden state runs through Expert 3's FFN and Expert 7's FFN only — not the other 6
The final output is 0.55 × Expert3(x) + 0.30 × Expert7(x), renormalized — a weighted blend of just two specialists, not all eight
Experts 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 do zero compute for this token, even though all 8 experts' weights are loaded in GPU memory

slides.title: When MoE isn't the right call
slides.body: MoE trades compute for memory and system complexity — that trade isn't free, and it isn't always worth it.
bullets: All experts must stay resident in memory even though only a few run per token — MoE models are memory-bound, not compute-bound, which hurts on memory-constrained or edge hardware
Expert-parallel serving adds real network overhead (all-to-all token routing) that a single-GPU dense model never pays
Fine-tuning is trickier: naive fine-tuning can cause routing collapse, where the gate stops exploring and overfits to a handful of experts
For small models or latency-critical single-request serving with no multi-GPU setup, a dense model is often simpler and just as fast in practice

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MoE's real contribution is decoupling two numbers that used to move together: how much a model knows, and how much compute it costs per token.
bullets: Router + sparse experts let total capacity scale ahead of per-token FLOPs — DeepSeek-V3 runs only ~5.5% of its 671B params per token
The bill doesn't disappear — it shifts from compute to memory and cross-device communication
Load balancing and routing stability are the hard engineering problems, not the gating math itself

questions.prompt: In a Mixture of Experts layer, what determines which expert FFNs process a given token?
options: Every expert always processes every token, just with different weights
A learned router/gating network scores all experts and selects only the top-k for that token
Experts are assigned randomly at each forward pass
The token's position in the sequence fixes which expert it uses
questions.explanation: A small gating network scores every expert for each token and routes it to only the top-k highest-scoring experts (commonly k=1 or k=2), whose outputs are combined by a weighted sum of the gate's scores.

questions.prompt: Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total parameters but only about 12.9B active per token. What causes that gap?
options: The model compresses weights at inference time
Most layers are shared, so only the output layer differs between experts
Only the top-2 of 8 experts run per token in each MoE layer — the other 6 experts' weights sit in memory but do no compute for that token
The gap is a quantization artifact, not an architectural feature
questions.explanation: Mixtral's router activates only 2 of its 8 experts per token per MoE layer. The other 6 experts still occupy GPU memory but perform zero FLOPs for that token, which is exactly why total and active parameter counts diverge.

questions.prompt: Why might a team choose a dense model over an MoE model despite MoE's lower FLOPs per token?
options: Dense models are always more accurate than MoE models
MoE models require all experts to stay resident in memory and add cross-device routing overhead in distributed serving, which can hurt on memory-constrained or single-GPU setups
Dense models don't require a router at all, so they can't support multiple tasks
MoE models cannot be fine-tuned under any circumstances
questions.explanation: MoE lowers compute per token but doesn't lower memory footprint — all experts must be loaded — and expert-parallel serving adds all-to-all communication overhead. On memory-constrained or single-GPU deployments, a simpler dense model can be the more practical choice.

posts.title: Dreaming: How AI Agents Consolidate Memory Offline
posts.subtitle: Claude's biggest memory gains come from an offline pass, not better retrieval.
posts.summary: Writing notes while an agent works isn't enough — Anthropic's 'dreaming' research shows the real gains come from an offline pass that checks those notes against the raw transcript before trusting them. Across CL-Bench 1.0 and a Pokémon Red benchmark, the agents that curated the least memory beat the ones that wrote the most.

slides.title: Agents Have a Memory Problem Retrieval Alone Can't Fix
slides.body: Anthropic's November 2026 'dreaming' research argues that writing notes while working isn't enough — agents need an offline pass to fix mistakes, the way the hippocampus replays experience into the neocortex during sleep.
bullets: The idea borrows from 'sleep-time compute' (Letta, UC Berkeley): let a model work on memory when it isn't working on a task
On CL-Bench 1.0, every tested model scored higher with a memory store than without — gains ranged from 0.03 to 0.28 depending on the model
But raw memory can mislead a weak model just as easily as it helps a strong one

slides.title: Writing a Note Is a Bet You'll Need It Again
slides.body: Salience is the hard part — an agent has to guess what will matter later without being able to see the future.
bullets: Agent memory specifically means knowledge kept between sessions — it excludes weight changes, in-context learning, and context compaction
Playing Pokémon Red, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders, then around step 10,000 spent 17 consecutive steps reorganizing files without taking a single game action
More memory isn't better memory: Fable 5 wrote just 9 files in 2 folders plus one dashboard note, and beat the game with 4 badges to Sonnet 3.7's 1

slides.title: Dreaming: An Offline Pass That Checks Memory Against the Transcript
slides.body: Instead of trusting a note the moment it's written, dreaming periodically re-reads the raw transcript and fixes, merges, or deletes what it finds.
bullets: Four-layer hierarchy: transcripts (full event log) → memory notes → representations like wikis → injected context loaded into every session
Dreaming moves information up that stack, verifying a note against the transcript that produced it before letting it propagate further

Worked example: a wrong note placed Pokémon's PokéCenter on the wrong side of Mt. Moon, so Claude walked off a one-way ledge and backtracked; after dreaming caught and fixed the note, Claude reached Cerulean City at action 1,935 instead of looping three times and turning back

slides.title: Wikis Beat Raw Search — But Only Combined
slides.body: On a roughly 350,000-file, 420M-token corpus, Anthropic graded 25 questions across 128 dreaming sessions, comparing search-only retrieval against a dreamed wiki.
bullets: On a harder 24-item merger-document task, the wiki alone scored 87% on multi-document, judgment-heavy questions vs. 73% for search alone — the more synthesis a question needs, the more a built representation helps

rows: Reads raw files fresh each time
Started at 13%, climbed to 48% as dreaming iterated
Best of both — also ~20,000 fewer tokens per question

slides.title: When Dreaming Breaks: the Map That Outgrew Its Territory
slides.body: A wiki is only useful if it's smaller and cleaner than what it summarizes — Anthropic found a case where it wasn't.
bullets: On one legal-document task, the dreamed wiki grew to 1.77x the size of the raw source corpus (203KB vs. 115KB), and some pages ended up with no incoming links at all
The team calls this the 'abstracted nothing' failure — a map that's bigger and less useful than the territory it describes

A separate failure: several agents writing to one shared table kept overwriting each other's facts, and the wiki held only 41 of 57 graded facts (72%) — until each contract got its own page with terms quoted verbatim, which hit 57 of 57 (100%)

slides.title: Telling a Model What to Remember Can Backfire
slides.body: Strict write rules like 'only record failures' hurt models that were already good at judging salience on their own.
bullets: Giving Opus 5 a strict write rule cost it 0.234 points of memory gain; Opus 4.7 lost 0.150; Sonnet 4.6, already weak at salience, lost only 0.020
The fix for weaker models was different: telling Sonnet 4.6 to read memory before answering and explicitly test its theories raised its score from 0.364 to 0.641
Sonnet 5 already reads its own memory before answering 9 times out of 10, unprompted; Sonnet 4.6 did so less than half the time — stronger models need guidance, not rigid rules

Open tradeoff: notes promoted into injected context cost tokens on every session and a wrong one propagates everywhere, which is why Claude Code's own auto-memory caps out at the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md

slides.title: If You're Building Agent Memory, Don't Skip the Offline Pass
bullets: Writing memory while working and consolidating it offline are different jobs — conflating them is why naive 'just save everything' memory underperforms
More notes isn't better memory: the agent that wrote the fewest, most curated files (Fable 5, 9 files) beat the one that wrote the most (Sonnet 3.7, 413 files)
A built representation (wiki) earns its cost on synthesis-heavy, multi-document questions — plain search already wins on simple fact lookup
Dreaming's biggest win was catching and fixing a wrong note, not writing more notes — build in self-correction, not just storage

questions.prompt: What does "dreaming" refer to in Anthropic's agent-memory research?
options: Fine-tuning the model's weights on past conversations
An offline process where an agent reviews its own transcripts to fix, merge, or discard memory notes
A random sampling strategy used at inference time
A method for compressing the context window mid-conversation
questions.explanation: Dreaming is explicitly distinct from compaction, in-context learning, or weight updates — it's an offline pass that checks notes against the raw transcript they came from before letting them propagate.

questions.prompt: In the Pokémon Red experiment, what did Sonnet 3.7's result illustrate?
options: It ran out of context tokens mid-game
It wrote the most memory (413 files) but spent 17 steps reorganizing files instead of playing, finishing with only one badge
It refused to play due to safety filters
It had no memory system at all
questions.explanation: Quantity of memory isn't the goal. Fable 5 wrote far fewer, more curated files and beat the game with four badges — curation mattered more than volume.

questions.prompt: Why did giving Opus 5 a strict rule like "only record failures" hurt its performance?
options: It made the model respond more slowly
It overrode the model's own, already-good judgment about what's salient, costing it measured memory gain
It caused the memory store to run out of space
Strict rules aren't technically possible to give a model
questions.explanation: Strict write rules cost strong models more than weak ones (Opus 5 lost 0.234 points of gain) — frontier models benefit more from loose guidance than rigid constraints, since they're already good at judging salience.

posts.title: Scion: Rebuilding Source Control for Agent-Scale Code
posts.subtitle: When 30,000 merges a day broke git, Anthropic moved the work from the client to the server.
posts.summary: Anthropic's coding agents started submitting more merges than any human team could, and git's assumptions — offline clients, local clones, packfiles — stopped fitting. Scion, their in-house replacement, shrank infrastructure 200x by moving history, blame, and merges onto an always-reachable server and keeping clients thin.

slides.title: 30,000 Merges a Day Broke Git. Anthropic Built a New Backend.
slides.body: When coding agents started submitting more work than humans ever could, Anthropic's biggest bottleneck wasn't writing code — it was source control.
bullets: Merged changes into Anthropic's monorepo rose from roughly 2,500/day in May 2026 to over 30,000/day by September — a 12x jump in four months
The main branch's history is nearly 100GB; a compressed working copy already runs over 25GB
At roughly 25 million CI checkouts a day, naive git fetches would mean over 600 petabytes of git traffic daily

slides.title: Git Assumes Offline Clients. Agents Are Never Offline.
slides.body: Git's design — distributed history, local clones, packfiles — optimizes for developers who might lose their connection. Almost none of Anthropic's clients do.
bullets: Anthropic ran several hundred internal git mirrors at peak just to keep up — and they got harder to operate as merge volume grew, not easier
Nearly all clients are agents and CI jobs that are always online, so paying the cost of a full local clone on every one of them is pure waste
The mismatch: git treats the server as optional and the client as the source of truth; agent-scale work wants exactly the opposite

slides.title: Scion Moves the Work to the Server
slides.body: Scion, Anthropic's in-house replacement for git on this monorepo, flips where computation happens.
bullets: Changesets, not commits: each one is a write-ahead log entry listing changed files relative to its first parent and pointing at content-addressed blobs — no git-style tree pointer
The server computes blame, path history, and commit-graph skip lists on demand from changesets through one generic 'derived data' mechanism; clients never see this machinery
A ref update (like moving 'main') is just a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row — completely separate from creating the changeset itself
Clients keep a bounded local cache and materialize only the files they actually read — no multi-gigabyte packfile, ever

slides.title: The Payoff: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper
slides.body: Anthropic measured the new system against the git-mirror infrastructure it replaced.

slides.title: Worked Example: an AI Rewrite Beat the Human Prototype
slides.body: Scion's own migration tooling became a case study in the shift it was built for.
bullets: A hand-written git-to-Scion ingestion prototype was handed to an early Claude Mythos Preview snapshot to rewrite
The rewrite used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster than the original — while preserving the implicit ordering invariants the migration depended on
Team size and timeline: 7 people built both Scion and its code-review tool, Antique, and finished the migration in 5 months — during the same stretch merge volume rose 10x

slides.title: This Isn't a Git Replacement — and Anthropic Says So
slides.body: Scion trades generality for scale, and that trade only makes sense under specific conditions.
bullets: Anthropic's own words: Scion is 'by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use' — its components are described as highly bespoke to this one monorepo
It assumes clients are always online; a distributed team of humans working offline on laptops is exactly the use case git was built for, and Scion gives that up entirely

The real engineering shift wasn't the storage format — it was workflow: traditional merge queues with global locks don't fit agent-scale commit rates, so Anthropic relies on post-merge and pre-deploy testing instead, with Claude fixing conflicts faster than humans can detect them

slides.title: The Real Lesson Isn't "Build Your Own Git"
bullets: The bottleneck that matters shifts when agents write most of the code: it moves from writing changes to storing, serving, and reasoning about millions of them
Client-server asymmetry — push computation to a server with a global view, keep clients thin — is the same lesson behind CDNs and DNS, now applied to source control
Source control as an API, not just a file-sync protocol, let Anthropic build automated bisect and revert pipelines that need no local repo at all
Anthropic isn't shipping Scion as a product — it's sharing design principles and says it will work with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community instead

questions.prompt: Why couldn't Anthropic just keep scaling git with more mirrors?
options: Git doesn't support monorepos
Git's design assumes offline-capable clients with full local clones, which doesn't fit an always-online, agent-driven workload at this merge volume
Git cannot store more than 10GB of history
Mirrors were cheaper to run than a full rewrite
questions.explanation: The mismatch is architectural, not a resource limit — git optimizes for a case (offline distributed clients) that barely exists in Anthropic's always-online agent fleet.

questions.prompt: What is a "changeset" in Scion, and how does it differ from a git commit?
options: It's identical to a git commit, just renamed
A write-ahead log entry listing changed files relative to its first parent and pointing to content-addressed blobs, without a git-style tree pointer
A compressed snapshot of the entire repository
A client-side cache of recent edits
questions.explanation: Changesets avoid git's full-tree-pointer model, letting the server compute derived data like blame and history on demand instead of storing it per-commit.

questions.prompt: What did Anthropic replace strict, lock-based merge queues with at agent scale?
options: Nothing — merges became fully manual
Post-merge and pre-deploy testing, relying on agents (including Claude) to fix conflicts faster than humans could detect them
A lottery system for merge order
Daily batch merges only
questions.explanation: Global locks don't scale to tens of thousands of merges a day, so Anthropic moved the safety net to after the merge instead of before it.

posts.title: Agent Lightning: Training the Agent You Actually Ship
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's RL framework trains your real coding harness instead of a rebuilt copy
posts.summary: Microsoft Research Asia open-sourced Agent Lightning v1.0, a ~3,500-line RL framework that trains production agent harnesses — Claude Code, OpenHands, mini-SWE-agent — through a model-call proxy instead of rebuilding their loops. On SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3.5-9B, it lifted Pass@1 from 41.8% to 56.4% while its Collocated Async RL design cut training GPUs roughly in half.

slides.title: Train the Agent You Deploy, Not a Rebuilt Stand-In
slides.body: Agent Lightning v1.0 is Harnessed Agentic RL: the same harness that runs in production — with its own context management and tool protocols — participates directly in training.
bullets: Open-sourced by Microsoft Research Asia, November 16, 2026
~3,500 lines of code; builds on the verl training stack
Works with mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex

slides.title: RL Frameworks Usually Demand a Rebuilt Agent
bullets: Earlier agentic RL systems (verl, AReaL, slime) assume the trainer owns the agent's interaction loop.
Real coding harnesses have their own context management, tool protocols, and execution logic that's costly to reimplement.
A reimplemented agent can behave differently from the one that actually ships — the thing you trained isn't the thing you deployed.

slides.title: A Proxy Watches the Model Calls Instead of Owning the Loop
slides.body: Point the agent's existing model endpoint at Agent Lightning's proxy. Nothing else about the harness has to change.
bullets: API Gateway: an OpenAI-compatible proxy that records prompts, responses, and log probabilities as rollouts.
Rollout Controller: runs the agent as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs — no paid sandbox service required.
Customized Trainer: built on verl; turns recorded rollouts into training batches through a sample adapter.

slides.title: Collocated Async RL: One Pool of GPUs, Not Two
slides.body: Rollout and model updates share the same GPUs. When an update starts, the gateway pauses new requests, lets in-flight rollouts finish, then resumes — invisibly to the harness.
bullets: Synchronous RL wastes GPU time waiting for every rollout in a batch to finish.
Classic asynchronous RL avoids that wait but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training.
Collocation gets async-level throughput from a single shared pool by pausing the gateway, not the GPUs.

slides.title: Rollout-Level Accounting Beat Per-Sample Accounting
slides.body: A harness can split one rollout into many training samples. Agent Lightning computes advantage and normalization per rollout, not per sample — and that choice showed up in training stability over 200 steps.

slides.title: 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified
bullets: Training data: ~6,000 samples built on the open-source SWE-smith dataset, run through mini-SWE-agent with Qwen3.5-9B.
SWE-bench Verified Pass@1 rose from 41.8% to 56.4% — a 14.6 percentage-point gain, with no change to the deployed harness's code.
The agent that trained is the exact agent that ships: same context management, same tool calls.

slides.title: Where the Claims Thin Out
bullets: Microsoft's own blog post doesn't quantify how other frameworks compare on size or cost — the 'lightweight' framing is the authors' characterization, not a head-to-head benchmark.
Kubernetes-native rollouts trade a paid sandbox service for operating your own cluster — real ops overhead if you don't already run one.
Results are reported on one model (Qwen3.5-9B) and one harness (mini-SWE-agent) on SWE-bench — generalization to other agents/benchmarks isn't shown here.
The proxy design still requires careful reward and rollout design; it removes the reimplementation tax, not the RL-tuning work.

slides.title: Observe the Model Calls, Don't Rebuild the Agent
bullets: A thin proxy in front of the model endpoint can turn any existing agent harness into an RL training target with near-zero code changes.
Collocated Async RL got roughly 2x speedup using half the GPUs of a synchronous setup by pausing the gateway, not the hardware.
Accounting at the rollout level — not the sample level — mattered for stable training when one rollout yields a variable number of samples.
Open source at github.com/microsoft/agent-lightning, with a technical report for the full method.

questions.prompt: What does Agent Lightning's API Gateway actually do?
options: It rewrites the agent's source code to match the training framework
It acts as an OpenAI-compatible proxy that records prompts, responses, and log probabilities
It replaces the agent's tool-calling protocol with a simplified one
It runs a separate copy of the model just for evaluation
questions.explanation: The agent just points its model endpoint at the proxy; the gateway transparently logs the rollout data needed for training without the harness changing anything.

questions.prompt: How did Collocated Async RL get async-level speed without a second GPU pool?
options: It uses CPU-only training for the policy update
It pauses new rollout requests at the gateway during an update, lets in-flight ones finish, then resumes — sharing one GPU pool
It skips the policy update entirely every other step
It runs rollouts on a cheaper, separate cloud provider
questions.explanation: Rollout and training share the same GPUs; the gateway pausing requests during updates is invisible to the harness and avoided needing double the hardware that classic async RL requires.

questions.prompt: On SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3.5-9B and mini-SWE-agent, what did Agent Lightning training change Pass@1 from and to?
questions.explanation: Pass@1 rose from 41.8% to 56.4%, a 14.6 percentage-point gain, using about 6,000 training samples from the SWE-smith dataset.

posts.title: Anthropic Cuts Its Bug-Disclosure Window to 30 Days
posts.subtitle: AI got too good at finding vulnerabilities for a 90-day grace period to still make sense
posts.summary: Anthropic shortened its coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines — the main window drops from 90 days to 30 (high/critical) or 45 (other), effective January 1, 2027 — because frontier models now find bugs, and rediscover the same ones, far faster than the old norms assumed.

slides.title: 90 Days Is Now 30 (or 45)
slides.body: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team announced new coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines on November 16, 2026, taking effect January 1, 2027.
bullets: Main window: 90 days → 30 days (high/critical) or 45 days (everything else)
Escalation to an outside coordinator if a maintainer doesn't respond: 30 days → 15 days
Full technical publication after a patch ships: 45 days → 30 days

slides.title: The Old Norms Assumed Human-Speed Bugs
slides.body: Anthropic says the 90-day standard, used industry-wide, rests on two assumptions that no longer hold.
bullets: Assumption 1: fixes move at human speed — but models now help write patches too, shrinking real fix time.
Assumption 2: a vulnerability one researcher finds stays private for months — but Anthropic reports a rising rate of independent rediscovery as models get better at the same search.
"Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities," the post states.

slides.title: The New Rules, With Carve-Outs
bullets: Actively exploited vulnerabilities keep the existing 7-day disclosure window — unchanged.
Hard-to-deploy software (e.g. critical infrastructure) or fixes needing a spec/RFC change get a negotiated timeline instead of a hard deadline.
AI-discovered findings that haven't had human review yet — like raw OSS Scanner output — aren't covered by these clocks at all.
Every report ships with actionable guidance, and where possible a patch or mitigation, not just a bug description.

slides.title: A Maintainer's Clock, Before and After
bullets: Old world: critical bug reported on day 0 → maintainer has until day 90 before any escalation pressure, patch, or public write-up.
New world (reports filed on/after Jan 1, 2027): same bug → escalation to an outside coordinator looms by day 15 if the maintainer is unresponsive, and the hard deadline lands at day 30.
Already-overdue high/critical reports (filed before the change, now past 90 days) get one more 30-day grace period before Anthropic publishes them on its dashboard.

slides.title: Old Timeline vs. New Timeline
The Programs Feeding This Pipeline
bullets: OSS Scanner: free, periodic scans of critical open-source projects using Anthropic's strongest models, with findings sent straight to maintainers.
Claude for Open Source Program: eligible maintainers and contributors get six months of Claude Ultra at no cost.
Cyber Verification Program: lets security professionals, including open-source maintainers, get access tailored to legitimate defensive work.
Anthropic says it will negotiate a sustainable pace with any single project before sending it a large volume of findings at once.

slides.title: Tighter Deadlines Cut Both Ways
bullets: A shorter window helps honest defenders patch before wider rediscovery — but it's also less forgiving for under-resourced maintainers of complex systems.
Hard-to-deploy carve-outs are judgment calls negotiated case by case, not a fixed number — expect friction over what qualifies.
This is Anthropic's own policy for its own disclosures, not an industry standard; other vendors and bug bounty programs can still run on 90-day norms.
The policy only governs Anthropic-reported findings — it says nothing about how fast any other AI lab's models find or disclose bugs.

slides.title: The Clock Sped Up Because the Search Did
bullets: Effective January 1, 2027: 90-day disclosure becomes 30 days (high/critical) or 45 days (other), with faster escalation and publication too.
The driver is capability, not policy fashion — Anthropic says rediscovery of the same bug by different models is rising.
Exploited bugs still get 7 days; genuinely hard-to-patch systems still get a negotiated timeline instead of a hard wall.
Open-source maintainers get real support alongside the faster clock: free scanning, free Claude Ultra, and a defensive-use access program.

options: 90 days
45 days
30 days
7 days
questions.explanation: High and critical severity issues get a 30-day main window, down from 90 days; other severities get 45 days.

options: Regulators mandated a shorter window
It assumed human-speed fixes and rare independent rediscovery — both assumptions AI has broken
Open-source maintainers asked for faster deadlines
90 days was never enough time to write a patch
questions.explanation: Anthropic argues models can now help write fixes (speeding remediation) while also finding the same bugs independently more often, so bugs no longer stay private for months by default.

options: Any bug found by OSS Scanner
Bugs in hard-to-deploy critical infrastructure
Actively exploited vulnerabilities
Bugs requiring an RFC or spec change
questions.explanation: Actively exploited vulnerabilities were already on a 7-day clock, and that stays the same — the new, shorter timelines apply to the main disclosure categories, not this one.

posts.title: Model Routing: Picking the Right LLM for Each Request
posts.subtitle: Why pay a frontier-model price for a one-line FAQ answer?
posts.summary: Model routing sends each incoming prompt to the cheapest model that can actually handle it, instead of sending every request to the same expensive frontier model. A router — rule-based, learned, or cascaded — decides per-request, trading some risk of misrouting for real savings in cost and latency.

slides.title: One Model For Every Request Is a Waste
slides.body: A support bot that answers 'what are your hours?' doesn't need the same model that debugs a race condition — but most systems send both to the same place.
bullets: Frontier models can cost 10-50x more per token than small, fast models
Most production traffic skews toward simple, repetitive requests
A router picks the model per-request instead of per-system

slides.title: Overpay or Underperform — Pick One
bullets: Route everything to the biggest model: correct more often, but latency and bill both balloon, often on traffic that didn't need it.
Route everything to a small, cheap model: fast and cheap, but it silently gives wrong answers on the hard tail of requests.
A fixed model-per-feature mapping doesn't adapt when a 'simple' feature occasionally gets a genuinely hard input.

slides.title: Three Ways to Decide Where a Prompt Goes
bullets: Rule-based routing: heuristics on prompt length, keywords, or detected intent (e.g. 'contains code' → bigger model). Cheap to build, brittle to edge cases.
Learned router: a small classifier model predicts task difficulty or which downstream model will answer best, trained on labeled or preference data.
Cascade routing: always try the cheap model first; escalate to a bigger model only if a confidence score or a verifier flags the answer as likely wrong.

slides.title: Where the Router Sits in the Pipeline
slides.body: Request → feature extraction (length, embedding, detected intent) → router decision → chosen model tier → response, optionally looping back through a verifier for cascades.
bullets: The router itself adds a small latency and compute cost — it has to be cheap relative to what it's protecting against.
Feature extraction can be as simple as token count or as involved as an embedding similarity check.
Cascades need a cheap-but-reliable signal that the first answer was wrong — a verifier, a confidence score, or a self-consistency check.

slides.title: An 80/20 Support Queue
bullets: Say 80% of incoming tickets are FAQ-shaped ('reset my password', 'where's my order') and 20% are genuinely novel or multi-step.

Routing the 80% to a small model at roughly 1/20th the per-token price of a frontier model, and only the 20% to the frontier model, cuts blended inference spend dramatically versus sending everything to the frontier model.
A cascade version: try the small model on all 100%, auto-escalate the ones it flags as low-confidence — catches misrouted hard tickets without hand-written rules for every case.

slides.title: Rule-Based vs. Learned vs. Cascade
When Routing Backfires
bullets: A misrouted hard query sent to a weak model doesn't fail loudly — it just returns a confidently wrong answer, which is worse than no answer in many products.
Every router hop adds latency; for latency-critical paths, that overhead can eat the savings you're chasing.
Learned routers need real labeled traffic to train on — cold-starting with no data means falling back to weaker rule-based heuristics first.
Multi-provider routing adds operational complexity: different rate limits, auth, and failure modes per model you route to.

slides.title: Match the Model to the Request, Not the Feature
bullets: Routing exploits the fact that most real traffic is easy; save the expensive model for the tail that actually needs it.
Cascades are the simplest reliable starting point — cheap model first, escalate on low confidence — without needing labeled training data.
A learned router pays off once you have enough traffic and labels to train one; until then, rules or cascades are good enough.
The router's own cost and the risk of silent misrouting are the real price of this optimization — budget for both.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind model routing?
options: Always use the biggest available model for reliability
Send every request to the same model but cache repeated answers
Send each request to the cheapest model that can actually handle it, deciding per-request
Fine-tune a single model on all traffic types
questions.explanation: Routing's whole value is making the model choice per-request instead of per-system, since most traffic doesn't need the most expensive model.

questions.prompt: In cascade routing, when does a request escalate to a bigger model?
options: On a fixed schedule, regardless of the answer
When a confidence score or verifier flags the first answer as likely wrong
Only when the user manually requests it
Every request escalates after one retry
questions.explanation: Cascades try the cheap model first and escalate based on a signal that the answer is probably unreliable, rather than routing by fixed rules upfront.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of a misrouted request in a model-routing system?
options: The request times out and is visibly retried
The system crashes and alerts an engineer
A weak model returns a confidently wrong answer with no obvious signal that it's wrong
The request is automatically sent to every model for comparison
questions.explanation: Misrouting typically fails silently — the wrong model still produces a fluent-sounding answer, which can be more damaging than an obvious error.

posts.title: TokenEconomizer: Teaching Coding Agents to Remember
posts.subtitle: A repo-aware plugin cut AI coding-agent costs up to 31% without touching the model
posts.summary: Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley profiled Claude Code on real repos and found agents waste a third of their tool calls repeating earlier work. TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin, learns from past sessions to cut costs 18-31% on SWE-Bench with no model changes and no accuracy loss.

slides.title: Coding Agents Forget Everything Between Sessions
slides.body: Every time an AI coding agent starts a new task in the same repo, it starts from zero — no memory of what worked last time, what tools it never needs, or what already failed.

slides.title: 30% of Tool Calls Just Repeat What Already Happened
bullets: Microsoft Research profiled Claude Code on 60 SWE-Bench tasks across real repositories.
After 5+ completed tasks in a repo, 30% of tool calls repeated an action already taken there — vs. just 7% across unrelated repos.
The agent received 23 tool descriptions per turn; 16 were never called.
The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of total spend.

slides.title: Three Lightweight Mechanisms, No Model Changes
bullets: Micro-skills: one-line repo facts, added to context only after several sessions confirm them, retired if later evidence contradicts them.
Tool pruning: drops tools repo history says are unlikely to be used; core run/edit tools always stay available and can be restored.
Failure-loop intervention: a judge model flags when the agent is stuck repeating a failure and injects a short redirect note.

slides.title: 18-31% Cheaper, Without Losing Accuracy
slides.body: Lowering the model's reasoning effort saved similar or more money — but caused substantial performance degradation. TokenEconomizer's savings came from skipping proven-redundant work, not thinking less.

slides.title: A Repo Learns Its Own Shortcuts After 6 Tasks
bullets: Tasks 1-5: the agent pays full price while TokenEconomizer's logs are still thin — sometimes pricier than the baseline.
By task 6, cumulative cost drops below the no-memory baseline in every one of the 6 repositories tested.
A micro-skill like 'this repo's tests need a setup step first' stops the agent from rediscovering it on task 12.

slides.title: Where It Can Backfire
bullets: Early tasks in a fresh repo can cost MORE while the system is still learning — expect a short break-even window.
The open-source failure-loop mechanism escalates stuck agents to a human instead of auto-stopping them.
Reported savings already include TokenEconomizer's own judge-model calls — the net number is real, not best-case.
Prune a tool too aggressively and you risk blocking a rare but genuinely needed action.

slides.title: Memory, Not a Bigger Brain, Cuts Agent Costs
bullets: ~30% of tool calls in a mature repo repeat earlier sessions — a real, measurable optimization target.
The cheapest lever (cut reasoning effort) hurts accuracy; the smarter lever (skip proven-redundant work) doesn't.
Open-source and model-agnostic — works on Claude Code and other agents with no fine-tuning required.

questions.prompt: In Microsoft Research's profiling of Claude Code on SWE-Bench, what fraction of tool calls in a repo with 5+ completed tasks repeated an earlier action in THAT SAME repo?
questions.explanation: 30% of tool calls repeated earlier actions in the same repo, versus only 7% across unrelated repos — showing the repetition is repo-specific knowledge, not generic agent chatter.

questions.prompt: Which baseline did the researchers compare TokenEconomizer against that saved similar or more money but hurt performance?
options: Switching to a smaller model
Lowering the model's reasoning effort
Removing all available tools
Caching every LLM response
questions.explanation: Reducing reasoning effort cut costs by a similar or larger margin, but caused substantial performance degradation — TokenEconomizer's gains instead came from skipping genuinely redundant work.

questions.prompt: Why might TokenEconomizer cost MORE than the baseline on an agent's very first tasks in a new repository?
options: It always runs with a bigger context window
Its tool-pruning mechanism is disabled by default
It hasn't yet accumulated enough session history to find patterns
It requires a one-time paid license
questions.explanation: The system needs several completed sessions before its micro-skills and pruning decisions have enough confirmed evidence to act — costs dip below baseline by around the sixth task in the repos tested.

posts.title: Google's New TPUs Split Security From Scale
posts.subtitle: TPU 8tx and 8i Max round out a four-chip lineup built for confidential and million-token agent workloads
posts.summary: Google Cloud announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, rounding its eighth-gen TPU lineup out to four distinct systems in one year. 8tx adds hardware-level confidential computing; 8i Max packages two chips for double the compute and bandwidth — but Google gave no pricing, GA dates, or absolute benchmarks.

slides.title: Four TPU Systems in One Year — A First for Google
slides.body: Announced November 9, 2026 on Google Cloud's blog, TPU 8tx and 8i Max join TPU 8t and 8i (unveiled at Cloud Next in April) to give Google four distinct eighth-generation TPU variants.

slides.title: One Chip Doesn't Fit Every Agentic Workload
bullets: TPU 8t and 8i cover large-scale training and low-latency inference, respectively.
Neither protects data or model weights while actively in use — only at rest or in transit.
Neither was built for million-token context or dozens of agents working across a full codebase at once.
Google says TPUs now serve nearly 100 customers — frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities — with sharply different needs.

slides.title: 8tx: Confidential Computing Built Into the Chip
bullets: Same silicon as TPU 8t, paired with 5th-gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts.
Keeps data and model weights isolated while actively in use — not just at rest or in transit.
Borrows TPU 8i's low-latency 'Boardfly' network: Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with near-zero performance penalty.
Lets a team fine-tune, distill, and run reinforcement learning on sensitive data on one system — no moving data between clusters.

slides.title: 8i Max: Two Chips, One Package, Double Everything
bullets: Packages two TPU 8i chips together for 2x the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of a single 8i.
Fits twice the silicon in the same rack footprint — more compute per square foot and per watt.
Aimed at dozens of agents working across a full codebase, or hours of video, inside one context window.

slides.title: How the Four TPUs Split the Work
A Regulated Firm Can Now Fine-Tune Without a Second Cluster
bullets: Before 8tx: a bank or hospital often had to move sensitive data to a separate, isolated environment to fine-tune or run RL safely.
With 8tx: fine-tuning, distillation, and RL on private data all run on the same confidentiality-hardened system.
Paired software: TorchTPU runs native PyTorch/Hugging Face models with no code rewrite; a new TPU agent suite plugs into coding tools like Claude Code and Cursor to autotune kernels.

slides.title: What Google Didn't Say
bullets: No general-availability date or pricing was given for either TPU 8tx or TPU 8i Max.
No absolute performance or memory figures — every number is relative to TPU 8i or TPU 8t, not an independent benchmark.
No customer or partner quotes accompanied the announcement, unlike most major hardware launches.
The claimed 'state-of-the-art' price-performance result cites a third-party source rather than Google's own published numbers.

slides.title: Specialization, Not Just Bigger Chips
bullets: Google now ships four distinct TPU variants instead of one general chip — security and context length are separate axes now, not features bolted onto a training chip.
TPU 8tx answers real demand from regulated industries that can't yet run sensitive fine-tuning on standard inference hardware.
TPU 8i Max's 'two chips, one package' approach is a density play — the real test is pod-scale pricing once it reaches general availability.

options: Faster training throughput
Hardware-level protection for data and weights while actively in use
Support for video generation
A built-in web search tool
questions.explanation: 8tx is built for confidential computing — keeping data and model weights isolated while they're actively being used, not just at rest or in transit — something neither 8t nor 8i offers.

Packaging two TPU 8i chips together on one package
Running at double the clock speed
Using a different CPU host

options: It didn't mention any software ecosystem

It didn't name the new systems
It contradicted the TPU 8t specs

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Fewer Keys, Same Smarts
posts.subtitle: The middle ground between full multi-head attention and memory-starved multi-query attention
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares key/value heads across groups of query heads instead of giving every head its own cache or forcing all heads to share one. It's why most serious open LLMs serve fast without the quality cliff multi-query attention can cause.

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention's Hidden Memory Tax
slides.body: Every attention head in a transformer needs its own key and value cache at inference time — and that cache, not the model's weights, is often what actually runs you out of GPU memory.

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention Caches One K/V Pair Per Head
bullets: A model with 64 attention heads needs 64 separate key/value caches per layer, growing with every token generated.
At long context lengths and large batch sizes, this KV cache can rival or exceed the memory the model's own weights take up.
Multi-Query Attention (MQA) fixes this by sharing ONE key/value pair across all heads — but quality can suffer, especially at larger model scales.

slides.title: GQA: Share Keys/Values Within Groups, Not Globally
bullets: Split H query heads into G groups; each group shares one key/value head, instead of every query head having its own (MHA) or all heads sharing one (MQA).
G = 1 reduces to MQA; G = H reduces to standard MHA — GQA is the tunable middle ground between them.
Llama 2's 70B model ships with 8 KV groups across 64 query heads — an 8x smaller KV cache than full MHA.

slides.title: MHA vs. GQA vs. MQA
slides.body: G is the dial: more groups trade memory for quality, fewer groups trade quality for memory.

slides.title: Why Fewer KV Heads Means More Tokens Per Second
bullets: Autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound: every step re-reads the full KV cache from GPU HBM.
Shrinking the KV cache 8x means roughly 8x less data to move per generated token.
That directly raises the batch size a server can hold in GPU memory — GQA is an inference-serving optimization, not just an accuracy trick.

slides.title: Serving a 70B Model: Why GQA, Not MHA or MQA
bullets: With full MHA, dozens of concurrent long-context sequences on a 70B model can push the KV cache into direct competition with the model's own weights for GPU memory.
Cutting to 8 KV groups (what Llama 2 70B actually ships with) shrinks that cache need roughly 8x, letting far more sequences fit on the same hardware.
Smaller Llama 2 variants (7B, 13B) don't use GQA — the memory pressure that justifies it mainly bites at larger scale and longer context.

slides.title: GQA Isn't Free — Pick G Carefully
bullets: Too few groups starts to lose the per-head specialization that gives MHA its quality — you drift toward MQA's weaknesses.
GQA is chosen at training time: you can't bolt it onto an already-trained MHA model without retraining or a conversion step.
If memory bandwidth isn't your actual bottleneck — short context, small batch — the serving win shrinks accordingly.

slides.title: GQA Is the Default for a Reason
bullets: It's now standard in most serious open LLMs because it buys most of MQA's memory savings with almost none of its quality loss.
The real lever is G, the number of KV groups — tune it based on how much you're willing to trade memory for quality.
Pairs naturally with serving techniques like PagedAttention and continuous batching: all three attack the same KV-cache bottleneck from different angles.

questions.prompt: In Grouped-Query Attention with G groups and H query heads, what happens when G = H?
options: It reduces to Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
It reduces to standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
The model stops working
It doubles the KV cache size
questions.explanation: When the number of KV groups equals the number of query heads, every head gets its own key/value pair again — that's exactly standard MHA. G=1 is the other extreme: MQA.

questions.prompt: Why does shrinking the KV cache directly speed up LLM inference, not just save memory?
options: Inference is bandwidth-bound — a smaller cache means less data moved from GPU memory per decoding step
Smaller caches use less electricity
It reduces the number of model parameters
It skips attention computation entirely
questions.explanation: Autoregressive decoding re-reads the whole KV cache from GPU HBM at every step. A smaller cache means less data to move, which raises achievable batch size and tokens-per-second for memory-bandwidth-bound serving.

questions.prompt: Llama 2 70B uses 8 KV groups across 64 query heads. What does that buy, and what's the catch?
options: Infinite context with no quality cost
Roughly an 8x smaller KV cache, but GQA must be chosen before/during training, not retrofitted onto an existing MHA checkpoint
A 64x smaller KV cache with no downsides
Faster training but no inference benefit
questions.explanation: 8 KV heads instead of 64 means roughly an 8x smaller KV cache — but GQA has to be chosen before or during training; you can't simply flip an existing MHA checkpoint to GQA without retraining or distillation.

posts.title: Experts Followed Their AI Agent's Lean 86% of the Time
posts.subtitle: A hidden-bias study found analysts rarely noticed when they were just agreeing with Claude.
posts.summary: Anthropic secretly randomized which side of four open methodological choices a Claude Code agent would argue for, then watched 50 expert analysts work through a real-feeling analysis task with it. Analysts matched the agent's randomly assigned lean 86% of the time, switched their own prior opinion 60% of the time when the agent disagreed with it, and mostly didn't notice any of it happening.

slides.title: Did You Decide, or Did Your Agent?
slides.body: Anthropic's alignment team ran a controlled study: can expert analysts tell when they're just rubber-stamping their AI coding agent's hidden preference?
bullets: 61 professional analysts used Claude Code to analyze a workplace program and recommend a decision
A coin flip secretly set the agent's lean on each open methodological choice — unknown to the analyst
Published Oct 27, 2026 by Anthropic's Alignment team (Herdağdelen, Joren, Tamkin)

slides.title: Four 'Judgment Calls' Hide Inside Every Analysis
slides.body: The task had no single right answer — it required four open methodological choices, each defensible either way.
bullets: Outcome measure: yield per hectare vs. per operating cost
Comparison method: difference-in-differences vs. covariate adjustment
Coverage (enrolled farms only vs. full membership) and weighting (equal vs. by producer size)
The board's bar for recommending rollout was a 3-4% productivity gain — a number sensitive to exactly which choices you make

slides.title: The Setup: A Secretly Biased Agent
slides.body: 50 analysts (of 61 recruited) used Claude Opus 4.8 at High effort inside a web-based VS Code environment; median task time was 65 minutes.
bullets: A coin flip set each agent's lean on each of the 4 decisions via a hidden system prompt
The agent was told to argue its lean honestly and change its mind if the evidence demanded it — it wasn't told to manipulate anyone
A no-lean baseline agent reproduced the same 5 choices in 112 of 123 runs, showing the task has a natural 'default-feeling' answer

slides.title: Analysts Matched the Agent's Lean 86% of the Time
slides.body: Chance alone would predict about 50% agreement across the four binary choices.

headers: Match rate with agent's assigned lean

slides.title: Worked Example: Flipping a Prior Opinion
slides.body: The clearest evidence of deference: what happened to analysts who walked in with their own opinion on a decision.
bullets: 38 analysts had a prior preference on a decision before seeing the agent's view
When the agent disagreed with that prior, they switched to the agent's side 60% of the time
When the agent agreed with it, they switched only 6% of the time — a 54-point gap (95% CI 24-82)
Final rollout recommendation: 54% of analysts recommended rollout when the agent leaned that way, vs. 36% when it didn't

slides.title: Confident, Credited Themselves, Still Deferred
slides.body: The deference wasn't driven by inexperience or low confidence — and analysts mostly didn't realize how much they'd leaned on the agent.
bullets: 90% of analysts rated themselves proficient or expert; experience, education, and self-reported trust in AI didn't predict deference
52% called the final recommendation 'more their own' than the agent's — yet deferred just as much as the other half
77% repeated the agent's arguments, sometimes verbatim, but only 15% credited the agent for them
Only 6 of 48 surveyed guessed the study was about AI influence; none suspected the lean itself was manipulated

slides.title: What This Means for Human-in-the-Loop Review
bullets: Human review only works as a safety check if the human's judgment is actually independent of the AI's
A no-AI control group made serious methodological errors 55% of the time (6 of 11) vs. 6% (3 of 50) with AI — but was less experienced, so this isn't proof AI improves judgment
If a team converges with a model that shares its bias, their 'consensus' may not be independent evidence at all
Practical mitigation the authors suggest: have agents surface open decisions and ask for your view before arguing a position

questions.prompt: In the study, what fraction of analysts matched the stance their AI agent had been secretly, randomly assigned?
options: 50%, same as chance
86% overall, significantly above the ~50% chance baseline
100% — every analyst agreed with the agent
Only on the outcome-measure decision (92%); the others were near chance
questions.explanation: Analysts matched the agent's randomly assigned lean 86% of the time across four decisions — far above the ~50% you'd expect from chance, showing the agent shaped choices it wasn't supposed to influence.

questions.prompt: What happened when an analyst walked in with their own prior opinion that conflicted with the agent's assigned lean?
options: They always kept their original opinion
They switched to the agent's view 60% of the time, vs. just 6% when the agent already agreed with them
They escalated the disagreement to a human supervisor
They ignored the agent's input entirely and worked independently
questions.explanation: The 54-point swing (60% vs. 6%) is the clearest sign of deference: agreement with a prior barely changed anyone's mind, but disagreement from the agent moved analysts far more often than it should if their judgment were independent.

questions.prompt: Why does this study's finding matter for AI safety practices that rely on 'human-in-the-loop' review?
options: It doesn't — human review is unaffected by AI agents
Because humans are always slower than agents at the same task
Because review only catches AI mistakes if the human's judgment is actually independent of the AI's — and this study shows that independence can't be assumed
Because it proves agents should never be used for analysis work
questions.explanation: If reviewers unconsciously adopt the agent's stance on contestable judgment calls — while feeling it was their own idea — then 'a human checked it' doesn't guarantee an independent check actually happened.

posts.title: KV Cache Quantization: Cutting LLM Memory in Half
posts.subtitle: Store attention history in fewer bits and fit more context per GPU.
posts.summary: The KV cache — not the model weights — is often the real memory bottleneck once you serve long contexts at high concurrency, because it grows with every request and every token instead of being a fixed cost. Quantizing it to FP8 or INT4 shrinks that cost without retraining the model, at the price of careful calibration to avoid losing precision on outlier channels.

slides.title: Your KV Cache Can Outgrow Your Model
slides.body: For long contexts and large batches, the key-value cache — not the model weights — is often the memory bottleneck on a serving GPU.
bullets: KV cache memory scales with context length × batch size × layers × heads — weights don't
Model weights are a fixed, one-time cost; the KV cache is a per-request, per-token cost
Quantizing the cache's bit-width is now a standard lever in serving stacks like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM

slides.title: Why the Cache Grows Faster Than You'd Expect
slides.body: Every generated token appends a new key and value vector, per layer, per attention head — and none of it can be discarded if the model still needs to attend to earlier tokens.
bullets: Size ≈ 2 (K and V) × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × bytes_per_value
At FP16 (2 bytes/value), doubling context length doubles the cache; doubling batch size does the same
Because it's per-request, the cache directly caps how many concurrent users — or how long a context — one GPU can serve

slides.title: Quantization: Same Vectors, Fewer Bits
slides.body: The fix doesn't change the attention math — it changes how many bits each stored number uses, with a cheap dequantize step right before the matmul.
bullets: FP16 → FP8 halves cache memory; modern GPUs (Hopper and newer) have native FP8 tensor-core support, making the dequant nearly free
FP16 → INT4 quarters cache memory, but needs per-channel scales for keys and per-token scales for values — a single global scale loses too much precision
Keys and values behave differently: key outliers tend to cluster by channel, value outliers tend to cluster by token — which is why the two tensors are often quantized along different axes

slides.title: The Memory/Quality Tradeoff by Precision

rows: Minimal — native hardware support, usually small or no measurable quality loss
Low if calibrated; naive per-tensor scaling can hurt outlier-heavy layers
Noticeable without per-channel/per-token scales; needs calibration

slides.title: Worked Example: Fitting More Requests on One GPU
slides.body: Say a 13B model at 8K context costs roughly 4GB of FP16 KV cache per request — on an 80GB GPU, that caps concurrency hard once weights and activations are accounted for.
bullets: At FP16 (~4GB/request): only a limited number of concurrent 8K-context requests fit after weights and activation overhead
Switch the cache to FP8 (~2GB/request): roughly double the concurrent requests fit on the exact same GPU and weights
No retraining, no change to the model's outputs beyond quantization noise — just more throughput per dollar of GPU

slides.title: When Quantized KV Cache Bites You
slides.body: Lower precision isn't free — it just moves the risk to specific failure modes.
bullets: Outlier channels in attention keys are sensitive — a bad quantization scheme degrades long-context retrieval first, since small errors compound token after token
INT4 or lower without careful per-channel/per-token calibration can quietly hurt tasks needing precise recall (long-context lookup, code generation) before it shows up in aggregate perplexity
Quantizing the cache saves memory, not compute — the attention matmuls still run at the dequantized precision, so it doesn't speed up compute-bound workloads
Combining it with prefix caching or speculative decoding adds complexity: cached prefixes must be stored and reused at a consistent precision

slides.title: When to Reach for KV Cache Quantization
bullets: Reach for it when you're memory-bound from long context or high concurrency — not when you're compute-bound
FP8 is close to a free win on modern GPUs; try it before touching INT4
INT4 and below need calibration (per-channel keys, per-token values) — a naive global scale isn't enough
It composes with other serving tricks like PagedAttention and continuous batching — it's a memory lever, not a replacement for them

questions.prompt: Why does the KV cache often become the memory bottleneck before the model weights do, at long context and high concurrency?
options: The KV cache uses a slower type of GPU memory
Weights are a fixed, one-time cost, but the KV cache grows with context length × batch size × layers × heads, paid per request
The KV cache always requires more bits per value than the weights
GPUs reserve a fixed memory block for the cache regardless of usage
questions.explanation: Weights are loaded once. The KV cache is a per-request, per-token cost that scales with how many tokens and concurrent sequences you're serving — which is exactly why it can outgrow the weights at scale.

questions.prompt: Why do keys and values often use different quantization granularity (per-channel vs. per-token)?
options: It's arbitrary and doesn't affect results
Key outlier magnitudes tend to cluster by channel while value outliers tend to cluster by token, so matching the scale factor's axis to each tensor's outlier pattern preserves more precision
Values must always use lower precision than keys
Per-channel scales aren't mathematically valid for keys
questions.explanation: A single global scale factor loses precision wherever outliers concentrate. Because keys' and values' outlier patterns differ, matching the quantization axis to each tensor's actual outlier structure keeps more useful precision.

questions.prompt: What does quantizing the KV cache NOT do?
options: Reduce memory usage
Enable more concurrent requests on the same GPU
Speed up the compute-bound attention matmuls, since they still run at dequantized precision
Let you serve longer contexts on fixed memory
questions.explanation: KV cache quantization is a memory optimization, not a compute optimization — stored values get dequantized back to full precision before the matmul, so it helps when you're memory-bound, not when you're compute-bound.

posts.title: Simulation-Based Inference: Letting AI Guess the Physics
posts.subtitle: Train a neural net on a simulator once, then get answers in seconds instead of weeks.
posts.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) trains a neural network on thousands of simulator runs so it can map real data back to the range of parameters that could have produced it — a distribution, not a single best fit. It's how modern AI pipelines are starting to build and constrain scientific models, from neurons to cosmology.

slides.title: A 3-Week Calculation, Now Done in Seconds
slides.body: In 1951, Alan Hodgkin solved his own nerve-cell equations by hand-cranking a mechanical calculator for over three weeks because Cambridge's computer was down. Today, a trained neural network does the equivalent inference in seconds.

slides.title: Fitting Data Isn't the Same as Understanding It
slides.body: A model that reproduces your measurements doesn't tell you it's the right model — usually many different parameter combinations fit equally well.
bullets: Classical fitting returns one 'best' parameter set and hides the ambiguity behind it
Exact Bayesian inference (computing the true posterior) is mathematically correct but computationally infeasible once the simulator is complex
Hodgkin and Huxley's famous nerve model used a term raised to the 4th power — they guessed it meant '4 particles must move' but had no way to confirm it for decades

slides.title: Train a Network to Invert the Simulator
slides.body: Simulation-based inference flips the usual direction: instead of searching for parameters that fit the data, it trains a model to recognize which parameters are plausible.
bullets: Run the simulator forward many times — ~100,000 runs for a Hodgkin-Huxley-sized model, millions for bigger ones — pairing each parameter set with its simulated output
Train a neural density estimator on those pairs to learn which parameter ranges produce which outputs
Once trained, feed it real data: inference on a new dataset takes seconds, even though the training simulations took weeks
This is 'amortized' inference — you pay the cost once, then reuse the trained network on any new measurement

slides.title: Three Ways to Fit a Model

rows: Seconds, after a one-time training cost

slides.title: The Hodgkin-Huxley Neuron, Revisited
slides.body: The 1951 model of a squid nerve cell's action potential is still the standard description of neuron electrical activity today — and it's a textbook case for what SBI adds.
bullets: Hodgkin and Huxley fit one parameter set by hand and hypothesized 4 particles had to move to open a membrane gate — pure guesswork at the time
Decades later, a solved potassium channel structure showed 4 identical subunits, confirming the guess
Run through SBI today, the same data would yield a distribution over plausible gating mechanisms immediately — showing which parts were actually constrained by the measurements and which weren't

slides.title: Agents Can Now Close the Whole Loop
slides.body: LLM-based agents can propose model code, fit it with SBI, compare to data, and revise — but the output should be a weighted set of models, not one.
bullets: A model-building agent writes candidate equations, fits parameters, checks the fit, and iterates

Because many different model structures can explain the same data, researchers report clusters of plausible models instead of a single winner — one published example split 41% / 39% / 11% / 9% across four distinct model families
The same logic scales to systems with 124,000+ neurons (a fly brain connectome) and beyond, where a single 'correct' model is unlikely to exist at all

slides.title: Where SBI Breaks Down
slides.body: It's a sharp tool for a specific shape of problem — not a general substitute for scientific judgment.
bullets: You need a working simulator in the first place; SBI can't help if you can't simulate the system at all
Training simulations can take weeks of compute even though inference afterward is fast — it's not free, just front-loaded
A model that fits data still isn't automatically 'understood' — large, flexible models can match measurements without being reducible to a few interpretable mechanisms
Most AI model-building systems so far have mainly rediscovered models scientists already know; evidence on genuinely open questions is still thin

slides.title: The Point Isn't One Model — It's Knowing What's Constrained
bullets: SBI trades a single best-fit answer for a distribution that shows what the data actually rules in or out
It's already used for neutron-star collision localization, cosmology, and structural biology — anywhere you have a simulator but not a tractable exact posterior
Pairing it with LLM agents that propose and revise model structure turns 'fit the data' into 'map the space of models that fit the data'
Fitting is cheap to automate; deciding what a model means is still the hard, mostly-human part

questions.prompt: What does simulation-based inference (SBI) return, compared to classical curve-fitting?
options: A single best-fit parameter set, just computed faster
A distribution over the parameter sets that could plausibly explain the data
The exact simulator code that generated the data
A ranked list of alternative simulators to try
questions.explanation: Classical fitting hides ambiguity behind one 'best' answer. SBI trains a network to recognize the full range of parameters consistent with the data, which is the real value — it shows what's actually constrained.

questions.prompt: Why did Hodgkin and Huxley's '4th power' term stay just a hypothesis for decades?
options: Because the math was wrong and had to be redone
Because no computer existed to run the calculation at all
Because confirming it required independent structural evidence (the channel's actual 4-subunit shape), not just a better fit to the electrical data
Because the model was later proven false
questions.explanation: The electrical data alone couldn't distinguish '4 particles' from other explanations that fit equally well. It took a solved protein structure, found decades later, to confirm the mechanism — exactly the kind of ambiguity SBI is built to expose up front.

questions.prompt: What's the core computational tradeoff of SBI?
options: It's cheap to train and expensive to reuse
It requires expensive upfront simulation and training, but inference on new data afterward is fast ('amortized')
It eliminates the need for a simulator entirely
It only works on linear models
questions.explanation: Generating hundreds of thousands (or millions) of simulation runs and training the density estimator is the expensive, one-time cost. Once trained, running real data through the network takes seconds — that's the 'amortized' part.

posts.title: Message Threads: Stop Resending the Whole Conversation
posts.subtitle: A new Messages API mode cuts first-token latency ~35% on long agent sessions — but not the token bill.
posts.summary: On November 2, 2026, Anthropic opened a public beta called message threads for the Claude Messages API: after the first request, you send only new messages plus a response ID instead of the whole conversation. For 500K–1M-token agent sessions it cuts median time-to-first-token by about 35% — though token usage and cost stay exactly the same.

slides.title: Your Agent Has Been Resending Everything, Every Turn
slides.body: A long-running coding agent at 800K tokens of context was re-uploading all 800K tokens on every single request — just to add one more message.

slides.title: Stateless APIs Don't Scale With Context
slides.body: The Messages API is stateless by design: every request carries the full conversation, including every past tool result and screenshot.
bullets: That's fine at 10K tokens — it's slow once an agent accumulates hundreds of thousands of tokens of history
Re-sending and re-reading the full conversation on every turn adds delay before Claude can even start responding
The problem compounds specifically for long-running coding agents, computer-use agents (which accumulate screenshots), and document-heavy workflows

slides.title: The Fix: Send a Thread ID, Not the Whole History
slides.body: Message threads add a `thread` parameter that lets the server hold the conversation between turns.
bullets: First request: client sends the full conversation and opens a thread via the `thread` parameter
Every later request: client sends only the new messages plus the ID of the previous response
The thread is held server-side in encrypted memory — not written to disk
A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request; after that, the client must resend the full conversation to start a new one

slides.title: What Actually Changes

rows: Only new messages + previous response ID sent
Full conversation still billed every turn — no change

slides.title: Where the ~35% Actually Shows Up
slides.body: Anthropic reports the 500K–1M-token benefit specifically for Claude Code, where message threads is already on by default.
bullets: A coding agent mid-session with hundreds of thousands of tokens of file reads and diffs: smaller requests, faster first response
A computer-use agent carrying a growing stack of screenshots across many turns
The article states the benefit grows with how much context the agent is already carrying — it's not a flat speedup for short chats

slides.title: Rollout: Public Beta, Multi-Cloud
bullets: Available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Models on Google Cloud
Direct API callers opt in with the beta header `message-threads-2026-08-12`
Claude Code has it on by default for most users already

slides.title: What It Doesn't Fix
slides.body: This is a latency optimization, not a cost or context-window optimization — don't expect it to do either.
bullets: Token usage and billing are unchanged: Claude still processes the full conversation every turn under the hood
It doesn't shrink your effective context window — long conversations still eventually hit the same limits
5-minute idle expiry means a thread isn't a substitute for your own conversation storage — you still need to keep your own copy to resend if it lapses
The announcement doesn't address zero-data-retention or HIPAA-configuration details; check Anthropic's docs before relying on threads in a regulated workflow

slides.title: A Narrow Fix for a Specific Pain Point
bullets: Message threads trade a bigger request body for a server-held conversation state, cutting time-to-first-token on big-context agent sessions
It's a latency win, not a cost win — budget and context-window planning don't change
Best fit: long-running coding agents, computer-use agents, and document-heavy multi-turn workflows, not short chats
5-minute expiry means your client still needs to hold the real conversation history as a fallback

The size of the model's context window
Time to first token on long, high-context requests
The number of tool calls an agent can make
questions.explanation: Anthropic reports about a 35% drop in median time-to-first-token for 500K–1M-token requests. Token usage and cost are explicitly unchanged — Claude still reads the full conversation every turn.

Anthropic automatically bills a cancellation fee
The thread pauses and resumes exactly where it left off

A long-running coding agent or computer-use agent with hundreds of thousands of tokens of accumulated context
A batch job that never reuses context
A request that doesn't use the Messages API
