posts.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs: Proving It Without Showing It
posts.subtitle: How you can convince someone a statement is true without revealing why.
posts.summary: A zero-knowledge proof lets a prover convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond that one fact. The idea, decades old in theory, now underpins practical systems — from privacy-preserving blockchains to zkVMs like Microsoft's Magnetar that prove a program ran correctly without re-executing it.

slides.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs: Proving It Without Showing It
slides.body: A zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) lets you prove a statement is true to someone else without giving them any information beyond 'it's true.' No password, no secret, no underlying data — just confidence.
bullets: Prove you know a secret without revealing the secret
Prove a computation ran correctly without re-running it
Foundational to modern privacy tech and verifiable computing

slides.title: Proving something usually means showing your work
slides.body: Normally, to convince someone you know a fact or ran a computation correctly, you show them the evidence directly — which means they now have it too.
bullets: Proving you're over 21 by showing your full ID exposes your birthdate, address, and name
Proving a password is correct by sending it lets the recipient (or an eavesdropper) steal it
Proving a program executed correctly by letting someone re-run it means they need your inputs, your code, and the compute

slides.title: Three properties make it a zero-knowledge proof
slides.body: A real ZKP protocol must satisfy three guarantees simultaneously — drop any one and it isn't a zero-knowledge proof anymore.
bullets: Completeness: if the statement is true, an honest prover can always convince an honest verifier
Soundness: if the statement is false, a cheating prover can only fool the verifier with vanishingly small probability
Zero-knowledge: the verifier learns nothing beyond the fact that the statement is true — no amount of transcript-watching reveals the secret

slides.title: The classic intuition: Ali Baba's cave
slides.body: The textbook example uses a circular cave with a magic door at the back, unlockable only with a secret word, and two paths (A and B) leading to it from the entrance.
bullets: Prover walks into the cave and picks path A or B at random, out of the verifier's sight
Verifier shouts which path (A or B) they want the prover to come back out of
If the prover knows the secret word, they can always open the door and exit from whichever path was called — a prover who's guessing wrong has a 50% chance of being caught each round
Repeat 20 rounds: a cheating prover's odds of surviving undetected drop to about 1 in a million

slides.title: Worked example: zkVMs prove whole programs, not just secrets
slides.body: Modern 'succinct' zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs/zk-STARKs) extend the same idea from 'I know a secret' to 'this entire program executed correctly' — the basis of zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs).
bullets: A zkVM like Magnetar runs a program once, then emits a short proof of correct execution
Anyone can verify that proof in milliseconds, without re-running the program or trusting the original executor
This is what lets a blockchain validator check a transaction's correctness without redoing all the computation themselves

slides.title: Tradeoffs: zero-knowledge isn't free
slides.body: ZKPs buy privacy and trustlessness, but every real system pays for it somewhere — in compute, complexity, or cryptographic assumptions.
bullets: Proof generation is typically far more expensive than the original computation (modern zkVMs narrow this gap but don't erase it)
Some practical schemes need a one-time 'trusted setup' ceremony — if compromised, soundness can break
Picking the wrong cryptographic foundation (e.g. elliptic curves) can leave a system vulnerable to future quantum computers
Zero-knowledge hides the 'why'; it doesn't replace authorization or access control for the 'what'

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Zero-knowledge proofs reframe trust: instead of 'show me the data,' the question becomes 'convince me without the data.'
bullets: Three properties define a real ZKP: completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge — all three, together
The same core idea scales from 'prove you know a password' to 'prove a whole program ran correctly'
Watch for where a system's security assumption actually lives (hash functions vs. elliptic curves) — it decides whether the proof survives future attacks

questions.prompt: Which three properties must a protocol have to count as a zero-knowledge proof?
options: Speed, cost-efficiency, and scalability
Completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge
Encryption, authentication, and compression
Decentralization, immutability, and consensus
questions.explanation: A protocol is a zero-knowledge proof only if it's complete (true statements can always be proven), sound (false statements can't be proven, except with negligible probability), and zero-knowledge (the verifier learns nothing beyond the statement's truth).

questions.prompt: In the Ali Baba's cave analogy, why does repeating the challenge many rounds matter?
options: It makes the secret word easier to guess
Each round a cheating prover survives has only a 50% chance; repeating rounds drives the odds of an impostor fooling the verifier down exponentially
It's purely for dramatic effect and has no mathematical purpose
It lets the verifier learn the secret word gradually
questions.explanation: A prover who doesn't know the secret has only a 50% chance of guessing which exit the verifier will call correctly. Repeating the challenge across many independent rounds compounds that uncertainty, making the probability of consistently fooling the verifier vanishingly small — without ever revealing the secret itself.

questions.prompt: What does a zkVM like Magnetar let you avoid doing?
options: Avoid writing any code at all
Avoid re-running a program yourself (or trusting whoever did) to confirm it executed correctly — you verify a short proof instead
Avoid using hash functions in your security design
Avoid needing a verifier entirely
questions.explanation: A zkVM proves that a program's execution was correct and produces a compact proof. Anyone can check that proof quickly, which means they don't need to re-execute the original computation or simply trust the party who ran it.

posts.title: vLLM 0.33: A Decisions Endpoint, Not Just Tokens
posts.subtitle: 927 commits turn an inference server into a structured-output platform.
posts.summary: vLLM v0.33.0 adds a /v1/decisions endpoint for structured yes/no and scoring queries, exposes token embeddings on /v1/embeddings, and refines speculative decoding with a lossy verification mode and quantized draft heads. It also removes Medusa and the MLP speculator, so upgraders need to check their speculative-decoding config.

slides.title: vLLM 0.33: A Decisions Endpoint, Not Just Tokens
slides.body: Released in early November 2026: 927 commits from 389 contributors turn vLLM from a pure token server into something closer to a structured-inference platform.
bullets: 927 commits, 389 contributors
New /v1/decisions endpoint
Faster, more flexible speculative decoding

slides.title: A full generate() call is overkill for a yes/no answer
slides.body: Classification, moderation, and scoring tasks only need one bit of information, but a standard LLM server still runs the full autoregressive decode loop to produce it.
bullets: Each token still costs a forward pass, even for a 1-token answer
Chat-completion APIs weren't built for structured choice/score queries
Teams hand-rolled prompt hacks ('reply only Y or N') to fake a decision API

slides.title: A dedicated endpoint for choices, not chat
slides.body: v0.33 adds POST /v1/decisions, which answers choice, yes/no, and score-style questions directly over structured state, and exposes raw token embeddings on /v1/embeddings.
bullets: /v1/decisions: structured answers without a full chat completion
/v1/embeddings now returns token-level embeddings, not just pooled vectors
Both reuse the already-loaded model weights, no separate embedding server needed

slides.title: Speculative decoding gets a precision/speed dial
slides.body: Draft-and-verify speculation got three additions: a refiner for block-diffusion drafters, an opt-in lossy verification policy, and a quantized draft lm_head.
bullets: Lossy verification trades exact output-distribution guarantees for higher accept rates
Quantized draft lm_head shrinks the draft model's memory footprint
New refiner improves accept rate specifically for block-diffusion-style drafters

slides.title: Three releases, three months, no slowdown
slides.body: vLLM has shipped a major version roughly every two weeks this quarter.

slides.title: Worked example: a moderation filter
slides.body: A content filter that used to call generate() and parse a short completion can now call /v1/decisions directly.
bullets: Before: prompt ends in 'Is this spam? Answer Y/N.', server still runs the decode loop and you parse the string
After: a single /v1/decisions call returns the structured choice directly, skipping the token-by-token generation loop
Net effect: fewer round-trip tokens per check, and no brittle string-parsing of the model's reply

slides.title: Before you upgrade: what breaks
slides.body: v0.33 removes two older speculative-decoding backends and a legacy executor outright.
bullets: Medusa and the MLP speculator are removed — migrate to a supported speculator (e.g. the new block-diffusion refiner)
The legacy Ray compiled-graph executor is removed
LM Format Enforcer is deprecated for structured output
CUDA 12.9 wheels are no longer published — CUDA 13.0 is now the default

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: vLLM is iterating fast and treating structured output as a first-class serving primitive, not a prompting trick.
bullets: If you serve classification/scoring workloads, /v1/decisions can replace a full chat-completion round trip
Lossy speculative verification is a real throughput knob — opt in deliberately, don't default to it
Check your speculator config before upgrading: Medusa and the MLP speculator are gone

questions.prompt: What problem does vLLM's new /v1/decisions endpoint target?
options: Running a full autoregressive generate() call just to get a structured yes/no or score answer
Training a new embedding model from scratch
Replacing the CUDA kernel compiler
Compressing the vector index used by a RAG pipeline
questions.explanation: Classification and scoring tasks only need a small structured answer, but previously had to go through the full token-by-token decode loop of a chat completion. /v1/decisions answers choice/yes-no/score queries directly over the loaded model's structured state.

questions.prompt: Which speculative-decoding backends were removed as breaking changes in v0.33.0?
options: FlashAttention and PagedAttention
Continuous batching and chunked prefill
Medusa and the MLP speculator
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism
questions.explanation: v0.33.0 removed the Medusa speculator and the MLP speculator entirely, alongside the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor. Teams relying on either need to migrate to a currently supported speculative-decoding method before upgrading.

questions.prompt: What's the actual tradeoff of the new opt-in 'lossy verification policy' for speculative decoding?
options: It uses more GPU memory in exchange for no benefit
It gives up the usual guarantee that speculative decoding's output matches standard decoding exactly, in exchange for a higher accept rate and more throughput
It only works on CPU inference
It disables quantization entirely
questions.explanation: Standard speculative decoding uses rejection sampling so its output distribution is mathematically identical to normal decoding. The lossy policy relaxes that guarantee on purpose, accepting more draft tokens for speed at the cost of exactness — which is why it's opt-in, not default.

posts.title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval That Knows When to Stop
posts.subtitle: Naive RAG searches once. Agentic RAG searches, checks its own work, and searches again.
posts.summary: Naive RAG embeds the user's question, runs one vector search, and stuffs the top-k chunks into the prompt — which breaks on multi-hop questions. Agentic RAG wraps retrieval in an agent loop that decomposes the query, grades whether results are sufficient, and searches again if not, at the cost of extra latency and LLM calls.

slides.title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval That Knows When to Stop
slides.body: Standard RAG does exactly one search per question. Agentic RAG treats retrieval as a decision the model makes, possibly more than once.
bullets: One fixed search vs. a search-grade-repeat loop
Built for multi-hop and ambiguous questions
Costs more latency and tokens — not a free upgrade

slides.title: One search can't answer a two-part question
slides.body: A single top-k vector search over the user's raw question returns one slice of the corpus. If the answer needs facts from two different documents, that one pass either misses the second fact or dilutes the top-k with irrelevant chunks.
bullets: Example: 'Compare Acme's 2023 and 2024 cloud revenue growth' needs two separate facts
A single embedding of the whole question often matches only one of the two years
The model then answers confidently using only half the needed evidence

slides.title: Wrap retrieval in an agent loop
slides.body: Give the model a search tool and let it decide when and what to search, instead of running retrieval as a fixed pre-processing step.
bullets: Query decomposition: split one question into targeted sub-queries
Sufficiency grading: a check (often a second LLM call) scores whether retrieved chunks actually answer the sub-query
Conditional looping: re-search or rewrite the query if grading fails, instead of answering on thin evidence

slides.title: The loop, step by step
slides.body: A typical agentic RAG pass runs five steps, repeating steps 2–4 until the grader is satisfied or a cap is hit.
bullets: 1. Plan — break the question into sub-queries
2. Retrieve — run the search tool per sub-query
3. Grade — score whether the retrieved chunks actually answer that sub-query
4. Decide — answer now, rewrite the query, or fetch more
5. Synthesize — combine verified evidence into one cited answer

slides.title: Naive RAG vs. agentic RAG

rows: Higher, variable — extra grading/search calls per loop
Can loop without a hard stop condition

slides.title: Worked example: the two-year comparison
slides.body: Question: 'What was the difference between Acme Corp's 2023 and 2024 cloud revenue growth?'
bullets: Naive RAG: one search for 'Acme Corp cloud revenue growth' returns mostly the 2024 filing; the model guesses or omits the 2023 figure
Agentic RAG: decomposes into 'Acme 2023 cloud revenue' and 'Acme 2024 cloud revenue', retrieves both filings separately
Grader checks both numbers are present before allowing an answer; only then does the model compute the delta and cite both filings

slides.title: When not to use it
slides.body: Agentic RAG is a cost, not just a capability — reach for it deliberately.
bullets: For simple single-document factoid lookups, it adds 2-5x more LLM calls for no accuracy gain
The grading step is itself a model call that can be wrong, compounding errors instead of catching them
Without a hard iteration cap, an ambiguous or unanswerable question can loop indefinitely, burning tokens and latency budget
Every extra loop iteration is a new point of failure to log and debug, not a free safety net

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Use naive single-pass RAG for simple, single-document lookups — it's cheaper and just as accurate there
Reach for agentic RAG when questions are multi-hop, ambiguous, or need cross-document verification
Always cap the loop (max iterations, confidence threshold, or time budget) and log each sub-query
Treat the grading step as a tunable precision/cost knob, not an automatic upgrade

questions.prompt: What's the main limitation of naive single-pass RAG that agentic RAG is built to address?
options: It can't handle multi-hop questions that need evidence pulled from more than one retrieval pass
It always runs slower than agentic RAG
It requires a different vector database
It can't use text embeddings at all
questions.explanation: Naive RAG embeds the question once and retrieves once. Multi-hop questions need evidence gathered across more than one targeted search, guided by what's already been found — which is exactly what the agent loop's decomposition and re-querying provide.

questions.prompt: In the agentic RAG loop, what does the 'grading' step actually do?
options: It retrains the embedding model on new data
It scores whether the retrieved chunks actually answer the current sub-query before the model is allowed to answer
It compresses the vector index to save storage
It ranks retrieval servers by network latency
questions.explanation: Grading is a sufficiency/relevance check — often its own LLM call — that decides whether the evidence gathered so far is enough to answer. If it isn't, the loop re-searches or rewrites the query instead of letting the model answer on thin context.

questions.prompt: What is the key production pitfall to guard against when deploying agentic RAG?
options: An ungoverned loop with no max-iteration or confidence cap can burn unbounded tokens and latency
It cannot produce citations for its answers
It only works with proprietary, closed-source models
It bypasses vector search entirely and reads raw files
questions.explanation: Because the loop keeps going until the grader is satisfied, an ambiguous or unanswerable question can spin indefinitely without a hard stop. Production systems need an explicit iteration cap or time/token budget, not an implicit trust that the loop will terminate on its own.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: When a Tool Needs to Ask You First
posts.subtitle: A server pauses mid-task, asks a real question, and waits for your answer.
posts.summary: MCP's elicitation capability lets a server pause mid-request and send the client a schema-validated question for the human user, instead of guessing a missing parameter or failing outright. Answers come back as accept/decline/cancel, and a 2025-11-25 spec revision added a separate URL mode so sensitive data like passwords or payment details never has to travel through the structured JSON path.

slides.title: Most Tool Calls Guess. Elicitation Asks.
slides.body: Model Context Protocol servers normally just return data. Elicitation lets a server pause mid-task and send the client a structured question for the human — then wait for a real answer before continuing.
bullets: Introduced so servers aren't stuck guessing a missing parameter or failing the whole call
The question comes with a JSON Schema, so the answer is typed, not free text
The user can accept (with data), decline, or cancel the request

slides.title: Agents Used to Fill In Blanks With Guesses
slides.body: Before elicitation, if a tool call was missing something only a human could decide, the model either guessed or the whole call failed — there was no clean way for the server itself to ask.
bullets: A guessed value (wrong AWS region, wrong file to overwrite) causes a silent wrong action, not a visible error
Failing outright burns the whole turn and forces the user to retry with more detail typed up front
Clients had no standard way to even render 'this server wants to ask you something'

slides.title: elicitation/create: A Structured Mid-Task Question
slides.body: During request handling, the server sends an elicitation/create request to the client: a human-readable prompt plus a JSON Schema describing the shape of the expected answer (string, enum, number, boolean).
bullets: The client renders its own UI for the question — a form, a dropdown, a dialog — MCP doesn't dictate the widget
The user's response is validated against the schema before it's handed back to the server
Each elicitation is scoped to that one call, not a standing permission the server can reuse later

slides.title: Who Talks to Whom
slides.body: Three hops, one round trip: server to client, client to user, and the validated answer back down the chain.
bullets: Server -> client: elicitation/create, carrying the prompt and the JSON Schema
Client -> user: renders a form in the client's own interface and collects the response
User -> client -> server: a schema-checked JSON answer, or an explicit decline/cancel

slides.title: A Deploy Tool That Double-Checks the Region
slides.body: Concrete scenario: a deploy_service tool call omits the target region.
bullets: Instead of silently defaulting to us-east-1, the server elicits: 'Which region should this deploy to?' with an enum of the user's actual regions
The user picks 'eu-west-1' from a rendered dropdown, not free text the model has to re-parse
The server only proceeds after a valid, schema-checked answer — avoiding the classic 'agent deployed to the wrong region' failure

slides.title: Elicitation vs. Sampling vs. a Plain Tool Result

rows: Ask a human a structured, schema-checked question mid-task
Ask the client's own model to generate or reason on the server's behalf
Return finished data; no pause, no question

slides.title: Where It Breaks Down
slides.body: Elicitation solves one gap and opens two new ones: sensitive data and overuse.
bullets: The 2025-06-18 spec bans sensitive data (passwords, card numbers) from the normal JSON-schema path entirely
The 2025-11-25 revision added a separate 'URL mode' that redirects the user to a secure out-of-band page for auth or payment instead of inlining it
A server that elicits too often turns an autonomous agent workflow into a chat wizard — every pause is a context switch for the user
Clients aren't required to support elicitation at all; a well-behaved server has to degrade gracefully when the capability is missing

slides.title: The Protocol Finally Admits Some Decisions Need a Human
bullets: Elicitation = structured, schema-validated server-to-user questions, not free-text guessing
Three outcomes only: accept (with data), decline, or cancel — no silent fallback
Sensitive data is routed through a separate URL mode, never the inline JSON path
Use it sparingly: each elicitation is a context switch the user has to pay for

questions.prompt: What validates the user's answer in an MCP elicitation request?
options: Free text parsing by the LLM
A JSON Schema the server supplies alongside the prompt
The client's OAuth token
A regex hard-coded in the client
questions.explanation: The server sends a JSON Schema along with the human-readable prompt. The client validates the user's response against that schema before returning it, so the server always gets a well-typed answer instead of parsing free text.

questions.prompt: Why can't a server collect a credit card number through standard elicitation?
options: JSON Schema has no string type
The spec requires sensitive data to go through a separate URL mode to a secure out-of-band page instead of the inline JSON path
Clients block all numeric form fields
MCP has no concept of sensitive data
questions.explanation: The 2025-06-18 spec bars sensitive data from the normal elicitation path, and the 2025-11-25 revision added URL mode specifically so auth and payment flows redirect to a secure page instead of traveling as structured JSON.

questions.prompt: What's supposed to happen if a client doesn't support elicitation at all?
options: The connection is terminated immediately
The server must handle the missing capability gracefully instead of assuming it's always available
MCP silently upgrades the client
The call succeeds anyway with null data
questions.explanation: Elicitation is an optional client capability. A server that depends on it without a fallback will break against clients that haven't implemented it — well-behaved servers check for the capability first.

posts.title: Agent Memory: Giving AI Agents a Persistent Past
posts.subtitle: Why every agent restart erases context — and the three-layer fix that stops it.
posts.summary: LLM calls are stateless, so without an explicit memory system every new agent session starts from zero. Working, episodic, and semantic memory layers let agents carry facts, decisions, and mistakes forward — but unmanaged memory introduces its own failure modes, from context poisoning to unbounded retrieval noise.

slides.title: AI Agents Forget Everything the Moment You Close the Tab
slides.body: A language model call is stateless by default — it only knows what's in the current context window. Memory is the layer that lets an agent carry facts, decisions, and past mistakes into its next session instead of relearning them from scratch.
bullets: Without memory, a coding agent that fixed a flaky test last week will happily reintroduce the same bug today
Memory isn't one thing — it's usually three layers with different jobs, costs, and failure modes
Done badly, memory doesn't just waste tokens — it can actively mislead the agent

slides.title: The Context Window Is Rented, Not Owned
slides.body: Even a generous context window is a temporary workspace, not storage — it empties out between sessions and fills up fast within one.
bullets: Context windows range roughly 128K-1M tokens depending on the model, but every tool call, file read, and turn of dialogue eats into that budget
Re-explaining a codebase's quirks, a user's preferences, or last week's debugging trail from scratch costs real tokens and real latency on every single session
A crashed or restarted agent process loses its entire working context unless something outside the model call persisted it
This is the core reason 'just use a bigger context window' doesn't solve memory: cost and attention both degrade long before the token limit does

slides.title: Three Layers: Working, Episodic, Semantic
slides.body: Most production agent memory systems split into three layers borrowed loosely from cognitive science, each with its own write and read path.
bullets: Working memory: the live context window itself — the scratchpad, current plan, and in-flight tool results. Gone when the session ends unless explicitly saved
Episodic memory: a timestamped log of what actually happened — turns, tool calls, outcomes. Written continuously, read by searching for 'what happened last time X came up'
Semantic memory: distilled, durable facts and preferences extracted FROM episodes — not 'user asked about dark mode on Tuesday' but 'user prefers dark mode'
Write path matters as much as storage: cramming raw transcripts into semantic memory just rebuilds the context-bloat problem one layer down

slides.title: Worked Example: The Flaky Test That Stayed Fixed
slides.body: A concrete before/after for why the write-then-retrieve loop earns its keep.
bullets: Day 1: a coding agent spends ~4,000 tokens of exploration tracing a flaky test to a race condition in a mocked clock, then fixes it
At session end, it writes one semantic-memory note: 'tests/test_foo.py flakiness caused by unmocked clock drift — see fix in commit abc123'
Day 5: a different session is asked to refactor the same test file. Before touching it, it retrieves that note via similarity search over ~40 tokens instead of re-deriving the root cause
Net effect: one 40-token read replaces a 4,000-token rediscovery, and the refactor doesn't quietly reintroduce the same race condition

slides.title: Picking a Storage Strategy
slides.body: None of these are mutually exclusive — most real systems combine a scratchpad with a vector store, and reach for fine-tuning only when retrieval genuinely can't keep up.

rows: Low, but hard to correct later

slides.title: When Memory Makes Things Worse
slides.body: Persistent memory trades one failure mode (forgetting) for several new ones.
bullets: Context poisoning: a stale or simply wrong memory gets retrieved and treated as ground truth, derailing an otherwise unrelated task

Unbounded growth: without eviction or decay, episodic logs balloon and retrieval precision drops as relevant notes get buried in noise — the same curse-of-dimensionality problem any nearest-neighbor search faces at scale
Cross-contamination: shared or poorly scoped memory stores can leak one user's data into another's session, or let a prompt injection plant a false 'memory' that quietly redirects a future session
Skip persistent memory entirely for one-shot, ephemeral tasks — it adds retrieval latency and attack surface with no session to pay it back on

slides.title: If You Only Remember Three Things
bullets: Memory isn't a bigger context window — it's a separate write/read system of working, episodic, and semantic layers, each suited to a different lifespan
The write path is the hard part: distilling episodes into durable, compact facts is what keeps semantic memory useful instead of becoming a second context-bloat problem
Unmanaged memory actively hurts: budget for eviction, scoping, and provenance, or a stale/poisoned note will eventually outvote the truth

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between an agent's working memory and its semantic memory?
options: Working memory is stored in a database; semantic memory never is
Working memory is the live context window for the current session; semantic memory is distilled, durable facts extracted from past sessions
They are two names for the exact same thing
Semantic memory only stores numbers, working memory only stores text
questions.explanation: Working memory is whatever is in-context right now and disappears when the session ends. Semantic memory is what gets deliberately extracted and saved so it survives into future sessions.

questions.prompt: An agent retrieves an outdated memory note and confidently acts on it, breaking an unrelated task. What's this failure mode called?
options: Context poisoning
Token starvation
Gradient collapse
Speculative decoding
questions.explanation: Context poisoning is when a wrong or stale retrieved memory is treated as ground truth, derailing behavior that had nothing to do with that memory originally.

questions.prompt: Why might you deliberately skip persistent memory for a one-off, never-repeated task?
options: Persistent memory is always free, so there's no reason to skip it
LLMs can't write to a vector store in a single-turn task
It adds retrieval latency and attack surface (e.g. poisoned notes) with no future session around to benefit from the stored facts
One-off tasks are not allowed to use a context window
questions.explanation: Memory's value comes from paying off across future sessions. A task that never recurs pays the write/retrieve cost and the poisoning risk without ever cashing in the benefit.

posts.title: Flint-Interactive: A DSL for Charts Agents Can Wire Up
posts.subtitle: Microsoft Research gives AI agents a language for building interactive charts instead of static ones.
posts.summary: Flint-interactive is a high-level language, released by Microsoft Research on Oct 22, 2026, that lets AI agents add clicking, filtering, zooming, and cross-chart linking to otherwise-static generated charts. A compiler turns raw UI triggers into semantic events and maps them to update operators, so neither the agent nor the developer has to hand-write renderer-specific interaction code.

slides.title: AI Agents Can Draw a Chart. Making It Clickable Is the Hard Part
slides.body: Microsoft Research's Flint-interactive, announced Oct 22, 2026, gives agents a high-level language for adding real interactivity — brushing, filtering, zooming, cross-chart linking — to the charts they generate.
bullets: Most agent-generated charts are static images or one-shot renders with no follow-up behavior
Built on top of the earlier Flint chart language, aimed squarely at both human developers and AI agents
Ships with Flint-MCP, so an agent can be wired to produce interactive charts directly inside a chat session

slides.title: Interactivity Is Expensive and Fragile to Hand-Code
slides.body: Microsoft frames this as a two-part failure mode that shows up whenever an agent (or a developer) tries to add interaction after the fact.
bullets: Cost: getting from a static chart to a working interactive one usually takes several rounds of agent reasoning, coding, and debugging — burning tokens and time on plumbing, not insight
Reliability: interactive charts commonly ship with broken hit-testing or bad layouts, and fixing one interaction tends to quietly break another

Root cause named in the post: existing visualization libraries' built-in interactions aren't expressive enough for anything custom, and there was no high-level language to specify interaction logic directly

slides.title: The Stack: Canvas, Compiler, Interaction Logic
slides.body: Flint-interactive separates "what should happen" from "how to render it," so neither the agent nor the developer touches renderer internals.
bullets: Flint Canvas: a state machine that tracks user interaction and manages rendering state for the whole chart
The compiler: turns raw triggers — clicks, drags, key presses — into semantic events tied to specific chart elements and their underlying data, handling hit-testing itself
Interaction logic: maps those semantic events to update operators — e.g. set style to highlight a point, set annotation to label it, set viewport to pan or zoom
A programming API exists for custom behavior: define a trigger plus a handler function that sequences chart updates, optionally touching external tables or app state too

slides.title: Worked Example: One Click, Five Linked Views
slides.body: The release post walks through concrete demos rather than benchmarks — the interactivity itself is the deliverable.
bullets: Gapminder linked brushing: brushing a set of countries in a 1952 scatterplot highlights the same countries in a 2007 plot of the same dataset
Dashboard linking: selecting "United States" in a table highlights its point in a bubble chart, surfacing GDP per person of $42,952 and life expectancy of 78.2 years
Climate phase portrait (DimpVis-style): dragging Seattle's point along its seasonal path re-syncs four other cities to the same point in the year — e.g. January at 4.2°C and 5.7 mm/day of rain

slides.title: What Each Layer Is Actually Responsible For
slides.body: Treat this as a map of where a bug or a new interaction belongs, not a performance comparison — Microsoft's post doesn't publish quantitative benchmarks.

rows: Never — this is what you're buying by using Flint
Semantic event → update operator (highlight, annotate, pan/zoom)
Wiring a built-in interaction preset to a chart
The built-in presets don't cover your case

slides.title: Where This Doesn't Help (Yet)
slides.body: The post is explicit about what it doesn't show, which matters before adopting it for anything production-critical.
bullets: No published numbers on how much the "several rounds of reasoning and debugging" cost actually drops by — the examples are qualitative demos, not a before/after benchmark
You're buying into the Flint ecosystem: value shows up most when agents or devs are already generating charts through Flint / Flint-MCP, not as a drop-in for an arbitrary existing charting library
The post doesn't state a license or link a public GitHub repo directly — it points to a project site and invites community presets, so production-readiness and support status are unclear
Built for structured, data-bound interactions (brushing, linking, panning); it's not a general-purpose UI framework for arbitrary app interactivity

slides.title: If You Only Remember Three Things
bullets: Flint-interactive's real contribution is a semantic layer between raw UI events and chart updates — that's what removes the hand-coded hit-testing and layout bugs
The compiler, not the agent, owns rendering correctness — interaction logic only ever talks in terms of update operators, never pixels
It's an Oct 22, 2026 Microsoft Research release with compelling demos but no published cost/reliability benchmarks and no confirmed open-source license yet

questions.prompt: What specific job does Flint-interactive's compiler do?
options: Trains the chart's underlying data model
Turns raw UI triggers (clicks, drags, keys) into semantic events tied to chart elements and data, including hit-testing
Generates the chart's color palette automatically
Replaces the need for a rendering library entirely
questions.explanation: The compiler is the layer that converts low-level input events into meaningful, data-aware events — so interaction logic can reason about "this data point" rather than "this pixel."

questions.prompt: In the dashboard-linking example, what two values does selecting "United States" surface?
options: Population and land area
GDP per person of $42,952 and life expectancy of 78.2 years
Stock price and trading volume
Temperature and rainfall
questions.explanation: Selecting a row in the linked table highlights the matching point on a bubble chart, which shows GDP per person ($42,952) and life expectancy (78.2 years) for that selection.

questions.prompt: What's the main caveat called out about Flint-interactive's release post?
options: It only works with Python
It requires a GPU to render charts
It shows qualitative demos but no published quantitative benchmarks on cost or reliability gains
It cannot be used with AI agents, only human developers
questions.explanation: The post demonstrates the kind of interactivity you get (linked brushing, dashboard linking, phase portraits) but doesn't publish numbers showing how much cheaper or more reliable this is versus hand-coding interactions.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Paying Full Price Only Once
posts.subtitle: A 100K-token system prompt doesn't need full-price reprocessing on every single call.
posts.summary: Prompt caching lets an API reuse the attention computation for a repeated prefix — a long system prompt, a shared document, a tool schema — instead of recomputing it on every call. Anthropic reports up to 90% lower cost and up to 85% lower latency on long-prompt workloads, but it only pays off above a minimum prompt length, needs an exact-prefix match, and the cache itself decays in minutes unless you pay more to extend it.

slides.title: Your System Prompt Gets Reprocessed on Every Single Call
slides.body: If a request sends the same 50-page document or the same tool definitions every time, the model pays full price and full latency to re-read them from scratch — every call.
bullets: Anthropic reports up to 90% lower cost and up to 85% lower latency for long-prompt workloads once caching kicks in
The mechanism: a server-side cache of the attention state for a prompt prefix, keyed to an exact byte-for-byte match
Available across the Claude API, Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry — each with its own minimums

slides.title: The Waste Is in the Repeated Prefix, Not the Question
slides.body: Multi-turn chats, many-shot prompting, and "chat with a document" apps all resend a large, unchanged block of context on every turn.
bullets: A 10-turn conversation with a long system prompt reprocesses that same system prompt 10 times by default
Many-shot prompting resends every example on every call, even though the examples never change
"Chat with a book" apps resend the entire book's tokens on every follow-up question about it

slides.title: How It Actually Works: Breakpoints + Exact-Match Lookup
slides.body: You mark where the reusable part of your prompt ends; the server checks whether it has already computed that exact prefix.
bullets: Mark a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the content you want reused — prefix order is tools → system → messages, and a change at any level invalidates that level and everything after it
A hit requires 100% identical content up to and including the marked block, including images — not semantic similarity, a literal match
The system also checks up to 20 blocks backward from each breakpoint, but only against entries earlier requests wrote at their own breakpoints
Up to 4 explicit breakpoints per request; automatic caching (when enabled) silently consumes one of those 4 slots

slides.title: Pricing: You Pay More to Write, Much Less to Read
slides.body: Caching isn't free — it trades a markup on the first write for a steep discount on every later reuse.
bullets: Cache write: 1.25x the base input price for a 5-minute cache, or 2x for a 1-hour extended cache
Cache read: just 0.1x (10%) of the base input price — this is where the savings come from
Breakpoints themselves cost nothing; you're only billed for actual cache writes, cache reads, and any uncached tokens
Mixed TTLs in one request are allowed, but longer-TTL entries must be placed before shorter-TTL ones

slides.title: Measured Impact by Workload
slides.body: Anthropic's own benchmarks show the gain scales with how much repeated context a workload carries.

rows: Multi-turn chat, 10 turns, long system prompt

slides.title: Worked Example: A Legal Agreement Reviewed 10 Times
slides.body: Say a 100K-token legal agreement sits in the system prompt, cached with a 1-hour TTL, and a lawyer asks 10 follow-up questions about it within that hour.
bullets: Without caching: all 10 calls reprocess the full ~100K-token document at the base input rate
With caching, call 1 is a cache write at 2x the base input rate for those ~100K tokens (the 1-hour TTL premium)
Calls 2-10 each pay only 0.1x the base input rate for that same block, since the exact prefix already matches the cached entry
Net effect across 10 calls: roughly one call's worth of base-rate tokens for the document, instead of ten — the same shape as the 90%-cost benchmark above

slides.title: Where Caching Quietly Fails to Help
slides.body: The exact-match requirement and minimum thresholds mean caching can silently do nothing — with no error raised.
bullets: Below the minimum cacheable length (512 tokens on current Claude models, up to 4,096 on some older ones), prompts are processed normally with zero error — check cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens, not your intuition

Put volatile content (timestamps, user IDs, anything that changes per request) at the end of the prompt, not the start — one changed token anywhere in the prefix invalidates that block and everything that follows it
The default 5-minute TTL is reset by every hit, but an idle gap over 5 minutes between calls still forces a fresh (full-price) write
Caching optimizes repeated-prefix cost and latency — it does nothing for the final, unique part of each prompt, which still processes at full price

slides.title: If You Only Remember Four Things
bullets: Put stable content first, volatile content last — the cache is an exact-match prefix, not a semantic lookup
Caching only pays off above the model's minimum length (512-4,096 tokens) and when the same prefix is actually reused within the TTL window
Reads cost ~10% of base price; writes cost more upfront (1.25x or 2x) — the payoff comes from reuse count, not the first call
Check the usage fields on every response — a silent miss looks identical to a normal call, just billed at full price

questions.prompt: Why should volatile content like a timestamp go at the END of a cached prompt rather than the beginning?
options: The API requires timestamps to be last
A changed token invalidates that block and everything after it, so putting volatile content first breaks the cache for the entire rest of the prompt
It makes the response format more consistent
It reduces the number of tokens counted toward the minimum
questions.explanation: Cache matching is an exact-prefix check. If volatile content sits early in the prompt, it changes on every call and invalidates that breakpoint plus every later one, so nothing downstream ever gets reused.

questions.prompt: A request has a cache write on a 5-minute-TTL prompt. What happens to pricing if that cached block is hit again 3 minutes later?
options: It's billed as a second full write
It's billed at roughly 10% of the base input price, and the 5-minute TTL resets
It's free, and the TTL does not change
It fails because only one hit is allowed per cache entry
questions.explanation: Cache reads cost about 10% of the base input token price, and every hit (or refresh) resets the TTL clock — the entry doesn't expire until it goes 5 minutes without being touched.

questions.prompt: A prompt is 300 tokens long on a model with a 512-token minimum cacheable length. What happens if you add a cache_control breakpoint to it?
options: The API returns an error
It's billed at double price automatically
It's processed normally with no caching and no error — check the usage fields to confirm nothing was cached
It gets rounded up to 512 tokens and cached anyway
questions.explanation: Prompts under the minimum length are silently processed without caching. There's no error, so the only way to know caching didn't happen is to check that cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are both 0.

posts.title: Proof-Driven Development: Verifying Agent Code
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's PDD Kit proves Rust code matches intent, not just that it passes tests.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's PDD Kit turns a developer's intent into formal Verus specs, proves an agent's Rust code satisfies them for every input, and falls back to tests for whatever can't be formalized. In a Pet Store case study, it caught a login bug that let one account's password unlock a different account's token — a bug nobody had read the code closely enough to spot.

slides.body: Coding agents now ship diffs too large to review line by line. Microsoft Research's PDD Kit answers with math instead of more eyeballs: formally prove the code matches what you asked for.
slides.title: When an Agent Writes 5,000 Lines, Who Checks It's Right?

slides.body: An agent that writes both the code and its own tests can satisfy itself without satisfying you.
bullets: Agent-authored tests usually verify the implementation the agent chose — not your original intent
Nothing in a typical agent harness constrains the agent to actually follow the plan it proposed
Gaps between intent and shipped code stay invisible until a bug surfaces in production
slides.title: Tests Check What Got Built, Not What You Asked For

slides.body: PDD Kit runs inside GitHub Next's Chopin environment and leans on the Verus prover for Rust.
bullets: pdd-plan: asks clarifying questions, then turns formalizable intent into Verus 'ensures' specs; the rest becomes tests
pdd-prove: Verus checks proofs deterministically (no model in the loop); an LLM reviewer hunts for gaps, and a mutation check plants one bug per clause to catch specs that constrain nothing
pdd-ship: Verus runs in CI next to empirical tests — a broken proof fails the build, same as a failed test
Trusted Computing Base (TCB): every piece the proof can't reach (hashing, the clock, DB lookups) is made explicit and signed off by a human
slides.title: Three Steps: Plan, Prove, Ship

slides.body: The target was Pet Store, a ~5,000-line Rust app (Axum, SQLite, Leptos/WASM).
bullets: Developer's request: two sentences about login behavior
PDD Kit generated 8 'ensures' clauses on login_flow across a 7-task build plan; 4 of them encode today's refusal rules
6 trusted pieces signed off: two DB lookups, check_password (a bcrypt wrapper), token generation, the clock, and error mapping
The proof caught a real bug: a path where login checked one account's password but issued a token for a different account — the developer had never read that code line by line
slides.title: Case Study: A Two-Sentence Request Became 8 Proof Obligations

rows: Only the inputs you thought to try
Every input the spec quantifies over
The spec you (and the agent) agreed on
No — a check that always passes still passes
Yes — mutation testing plants a bug per clause
"Seconds for a small module, up to minutes for a larger codebase"

slides.title: Proofs vs. Tests: What Each Actually Catches

bullets: Microsoft calls it a research prototype — Rust-only for now, with no PDD Kit repo link published yet
"A wrong spec is still possible": a sloppy or mistaken ensures clause gets you code that's provably compliant with the wrong thing
Proofs still take real effort — mostly in writing the proof itself, not running it
Guarantees are only as strong as the trusted pieces you sign off on — bugs inside check_password or the clock wrapper are invisible to the proof
Out of scope entirely: whether the login future ever completes, timing/rate of attempts, anything nobody thought to write down
slides.title: Where This Still Breaks

bullets: PDD Kit shrinks the review problem from 'read every line' to 'approve every trusted assumption'
The two-sentence-request → 8-clause-spec gap is the real deliverable: it surfaces what you actually meant
Mutation testing on 'ensures' clauses is the trick that stops vibe-verification — a spec that proves nothing still looks green without it
Treat this as an emerging pattern, not a drop-in tool yet: one language, one prototype, one case study
slides.title: Proof Doesn't Replace Judgment — It Relocates It

questions.explanation: The core problem PDD Kit targets: self-authored tests usually check what the agent built, so they pass even when the implementation diverges from the developer's actual intent.
questions.prompt: Why can't an agent's own tests be trusted to catch intent-vs-implementation gaps?
options: Tests run too slowly in CI to be useful
An agent that writes both the code and the tests can make the tests match whatever it built, not what was actually asked for
Rust doesn't support unit testing
Tests can only check compile errors, not logic

questions.explanation: The TCB makes explicit where proof coverage ends and human trust begins — in the Pet Store case, six pieces like check_password and the clock were signed off rather than proved.
questions.prompt: What is PDD Kit's 'Trusted Computing Base' (TCB)?
options: The cloud infrastructure running the proof checker
The explicit set of code pieces (like a bcrypt wrapper or the clock) the proof can't reach, which a human must sign off on instead
A benchmark suite for grading agent-written code
The subset of Verus that runs fastest

questions.explanation: By planting one bug per 'ensures' clause and checking the proof still fails to verify, the mutation check catches specs so weak they'd pass regardless of what the code does.
questions.prompt: What does PDD Kit's mutation check guard against?
options: Slow proof-checking performance
Memory leaks in the Rust binary
Missing documentation on proved functions
'Ensures' clauses that are technically satisfied but don't actually constrain anything — vacuous specs

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Missing Context
posts.subtitle: Prepending a few sentences of context to each chunk cut retrieval failures by two-thirds.
posts.summary: Standard RAG embeds each chunk in isolation, so chunks lose the surrounding information needed to match the right query. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval prepends a short, chunk-specific summary before embedding and indexing — cutting retrieval failure rate from 5.7% to 2.9%, and to 1.9% when combined with reranking.

slides.body: Split a document into isolated pieces and embed each alone, and you throw away exactly the information a search needs to know the piece matters.
slides.title: A Chunk Without Context Is a Clue Without a Case File

slides.body: Anthropic's own example: a chunk reading 'revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.'
bullets: That sentence doesn't say which company, or which quarter — it's true but unfindable
A query like 'What was ACME Corp's revenue growth in Q2 2023?' won't match it on embedding similarity or on BM25 keyword overlap
The failure happens silently at indexing time, long before anyone asks a question
slides.title: Chunking Throws Away the Referent

slides.body: Contextual Retrieval has two parts, applied before any retrieval happens.
bullets: Contextual Embeddings: a short, chunk-specific blurb (typically 50-100 tokens) is prepended to the chunk before embedding
Contextual BM25: the same contextualized text also builds the lexical/keyword index, not just the vector index
Claude (Anthropic used Claude 3 Haiku) generates the blurb by reading the whole document plus the chunk
Prompt caching loads the full document once and reuses it across all of that document's chunks — estimated cost: about $1.02 per million document tokens
slides.title: Prepend Context, Then Embed and Index

bullets: Original chunk: "This chunk is from an SEC filing... the company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter." (no company or quarter named)
After contextualization: "This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME Corp's performance in Q2 2023; the previous quarter's revenue was $314 million."
Now both the embedding and the BM25 index carry the company name, the filing type, and the quarter
The query 'What was ACME Corp's revenue growth in Q2 2023?' can match on vector similarity AND on the literal keywords 'ACME' and 'Q2 2023'
slides.title: Worked Example: The ACME Filing

slides.body: Measured as 1 − recall@20, best embedding model (Gemini Text 004), retrieving the top-20 chunks.
slides.title: Stacking the Techniques: Retrieval Failure Rate

bullets: Retrieve the top 150 chunks using contextual embeddings + contextual BM25
Pass the query and all 150 chunks through a reranker (Anthropic used Cohere's) which scores relevance in parallel
Keep only the top 20 reranked chunks to send to the model
20 beat both 5 and 10 in testing — more context helps up to a point, then starts distracting the model
slides.title: Where Reranking Fits in the Pipeline

bullets: Reranking every query adds real latency — there's a direct performance/cost/speed tradeoff in how many chunks you rerank
Gains are model-dependent: Gemini and Voyage embeddings benefited most in testing; not every embedding model gains equally
Chunk size, boundaries, and overlap still matter — contextualizing bad chunk boundaries doesn't fix them
If your whole knowledge base is under ~200,000 tokens, Anthropic's own recommendation is to skip chunking entirely and just put the whole thing in the prompt with caching
slides.title: When Contextual Retrieval Isn't the Right Tool

bullets: Embeddings are only as good as what's in the chunk — if the referent is missing, no embedding model can find it
Fixing it at indexing time (not query time) means every future query benefits, not just the one you're debugging
Contextual Embeddings + Contextual BM25 + reranking are additive: each layer independently cuts the failure rate further
It's a retrieval-quality technique, not a replacement for good chunking, good embeddings, or asking whether you need RAG at all
slides.title: The Core Idea, Compressed

questions.explanation: A chunk like 'revenue grew by 3%' is true but unfindable without knowing which company and quarter it refers to — that context lives in the surrounding document, not the chunk itself.
questions.prompt: What specific information does a plain embedded chunk often lose, according to Anthropic's example?
options: The formatting and whitespace of the original document
The referent — e.g., which company and which time period a standalone sentence is actually about
The language the document was written in
The file size of the source document

questions.explanation: The techniques stack: Contextual Embeddings alone cut failures 35%, adding Contextual BM25 reached 49%, and adding reranking on top reached 67% (5.7% → 1.9%).
questions.prompt: In Anthropic's tests, what was the failure-rate reduction when Contextual Embeddings, Contextual BM25, AND reranking were all combined?
options: 67%, taking the failure rate from 5.7% down to 1.9%
10%, a marginal improvement
100% — reranking alone eliminates all retrieval failures
35%, the same as Contextual Embeddings alone

questions.explanation: For small knowledge bases, the simplest fix beats any retrieval pipeline: just put the whole thing in the prompt and let prompt caching keep the cost down.
questions.prompt: When does Anthropic's own guidance say to skip chunking and Contextual Retrieval altogether?
options: Whenever using a reranker
When the entire knowledge base is small enough (under roughly 200,000 tokens) to just include in the prompt with caching
Whenever using BM25 instead of embeddings
Never — Contextual Retrieval should always be used for any RAG system

posts.title: Building AI Safety Evals That Actually Hold Up
posts.subtitle: Most safety evals are gameable, undocumented, or quietly measuring the wrong thing.
posts.summary: A safety eval only asks one narrow question: given this input, did the model do the right thing? Anthropic's engineering team lays out how to design, run, and grade these evals so the numbers mean something — covering multi-turn simulation, grader calibration with Cohen's kappa, and why single-turn refusal rates are already saturated at 94-98%.

slides.title: Most AI Safety Evals Don't Hold Up
slides.body: A safety eval measures a model's propensity to cause harm and how severe it would be — not what it can do, but what it does given a specific input.
bullets: Evals can be gamed, can quietly measure the wrong construct, and are often too undocumented to reproduce
Results shift just from multiple-choice vs. open-ended format, or from the order answer options appear in
Anthropic's Nov 2026 engineering write-up turns psychology's replication-crisis lessons into a checklist for eval design

slides.title: Refusal Is Often the Wrong Thing to Measure
slides.body: Counting refusals treats every "no" as a win — but for self-harm and suicide questions, a flat refusal can itself be the failure.
bullets: Dual-use domains (biology, cybersecurity) need a rubric that rewards helping with the legitimate version of a request while withholding operational specifics
Anthropic instead reports an 'appropriate response rate': in multi-turn evals, one bad turn fails the entire conversation
The same domain needs both a harmful-compliance check and an over-refusal check — optimizing only one just moves the failure mode

slides.title: Match the Design to the Question
slides.body: Two different eval shapes answer two different questions, and conflating them produces numbers nobody can act on.
bullets: Observational design: just describe behavior under realistic conditions — useful for a baseline, useless for proving cause
Causal design: vary exactly one variable (e.g. with vs. without a system-prompt change) to test whether an intervention actually helped
Vary scenario dimensions independently too — severity and tone crossed in the same scenario, so their effects don't get tangled together

slides.title: Multi-Turn Simulation, Step by Step
slides.body: Real harm often builds gradually across a conversation, so Anthropic simulates the whole arc instead of grading single messages.
bullets: A domain expert (e.g. a clinician for self-harm topics) writes a spec: the simulated user's goal, tactics, and dimensions like persona and tone
The first user turn is fixed; a separate Claude model generates every later turn, reacting live to the tested model's replies
Each scenario runs many times across dimension combinations, then a grader model scores the full transcript against the rubric

slides.title: Single-Turn Is Saturated; Multi-Turn Isn't
slides.body: On Anthropic's API, single-turn harmless-response rates already sit at 94-98% across recent models — the real signal is elsewhere.

rows: 94-98% — saturated, now mostly a regression check
Varies far more; CIs can exceed ±10 percentage points
Up to 34-point gap on the same multi-turn eval

slides.title: Worked Example: The Self-Harm System Prompt Fix
slides.body: Pre-release testing of Claude Fable 5.1 found Claude sometimes implicitly validated self-harm as a coping strategy.
bullets: Before the fix: appropriate response rate on the API eval was notably lower than on claude.ai, which carries its own system prompt
After adding a targeted system-prompt instruction and re-running: 60% on the bare API vs. 94% on claude.ai with the new prompt
The gap is the finding — it shows the model's behavior is highly sensitive to configuration, not just weights, so evals must test the actual deployed setup

slides.title: A Grader Is Only as Good as Its Validation
slides.body: An unvalidated grader model can quietly become the real source of error in the whole eval.
bullets: Validate against human labels with a chance-corrected agreement score (Cohen's kappa) — the grader should agree with experts about as often as experts agree with each other
Keep graders blind to design metadata, try a different model as grader, and check for length bias and position bias by flipping pairwise option order
Fail loudly: flag and exclude items where the grader itself breaks, instead of silently scoring them
Minimum sample sizes: ~100 items for complex multi-turn evals, ~1,000 for simple single-turn ones; run each case multiple times

slides.title: If You Only Do Three Things
bullets: Define the construct before collecting data — know exactly what "appropriate" means for this domain before you grade anything
Validate the grader against human judgment, not just against itself
Report uncertainty and break results out by category — averaging hides the one category that actually regressed
Don't compare scores across different graders, prompts, or settings — an improvement could just be a different measuring stick
Run evals continuously during training, not only right before release

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic report an "appropriate response rate" instead of a refusal rate for self-harm evals?
options: It's easier to compute automatically
A flat refusal can itself be the wrong, harmful response in that domain
Refusal rates can't be measured across multiple turns
It only applies to cybersecurity evals
questions.explanation: For self-harm and suicide questions, a blunt refusal can be a failure in itself. "Appropriate response rate" grades whether the model did the right thing for that specific, sensitive context — not just whether it said no.

questions.prompt: What does validating a grader model with Cohen's kappa actually check?
options: How fast the grader runs
Whether the grader's verdicts agree with human experts about as much as experts agree with each other
Whether the grader uses the same model family as the one being tested
The grader's token cost per evaluation
questions.explanation: Cohen's kappa is a chance-corrected agreement score. If the grader doesn't match human-expert judgments at roughly the rate experts match each other, the grader itself — not the model being tested — may be the source of the eval's error.

questions.prompt: In the Fable 5.1 example, what caused the appropriate-response rate to jump from roughly 60% to 94% on the same self-harm eval?
options: Retraining the model's weights
Switching to a larger grading model
Adding a targeted system-prompt instruction and testing the claude.ai configuration instead of the bare API
Lowering the sample size
questions.explanation: The model's weights didn't change — the deployment configuration did. The claude.ai system prompt plus a targeted fix closed a 34-point gap, showing why evals must test the actual deployed setup, not just the raw model.

posts.title: A2A: How AI Agents Talk to Other Agents
posts.subtitle: MCP connects an agent to tools. A2A connects agents to each other, across vendors.
posts.summary: The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, introduced by Google and now governed under the Linux Foundation, lets agents built on different frameworks discover each other's capabilities and delegate work through a shared task lifecycle. It solves a different problem than MCP: MCP wires an agent to tools and data; A2A wires one agent to another.

slides.title: Two Agents, Two Vendors, Zero Shared Context
slides.body: A travel-planning agent built on one framework has no built-in way to ask a specialized flight-search agent built on a totally different stack for help.
bullets: Without a shared protocol, every agent-to-agent integration is a one-off, custom API contract
That's an N-times-M problem: every new agent needs a bespoke connector to every other agent it talks to
Google's A2A protocol, now under the Linux Foundation, standardizes that handoff instead

slides.title: A2A Solves a Different Problem Than MCP
slides.body: They're complementary, not competing — most real systems need both.
bullets: MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects one agent to tools, files, and data sources it calls directly
A2A connects one autonomous agent to another autonomous agent, each with its own model, memory, and goals
Rule of thumb: if the other side can reason and make its own decisions, reach for A2A; if it's a function or a dataset, reach for MCP

slides.title: The Agent Card: A Public Resume for Agents
slides.body: Before delegating anything, a client needs to know what an agent can actually do.
bullets: Every A2A-compliant agent publishes a JSON "Agent Card" at a well-known URL, describing its identity, skills, endpoint, and supported auth schemes
A client reads the card first and matches its task against the agent's advertised skills — no guessing, no undocumented API
Cards can be cryptographically signed to prove origin, though signing says nothing about whether the agent behaves well once called

slides.title: A Task Has a Lifecycle, Not Just a Response
slides.body: A2A treats delegated work as a stateful Task that can span minutes or days, not a single request/response round trip.
bullets: States flow from submitted to working, then to either input-required / auth-required, or a terminal state: completed, failed, canceled, or rejected
input-required lets the remote agent pause and ask a clarifying question mid-task — essential for anything needing a human decision partway through
A client can poll for status or subscribe to a stream of updates, so long-running delegated work doesn't block the caller

slides.title: Three Transports, One Behavior
slides.body: The spec defines multiple wire formats so teams can fit A2A into whatever stack they already run.
bullets: JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTPS, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON/REST are all supported bindings, required to behave equivalently
JSON-RPC over HTTPS is the most common deployment in practice — simple to add to an existing HTTP service
Because the bindings are equivalent, an agent written against one transport can still be reached by a client that only speaks another

slides.title: Worked Example: Delegating a Flight Search
slides.body: A trip-planning agent needs live fares it doesn't have direct access to.
bullets: 1. It fetches the flight-search agent's Agent Card and finds a 'search_flights' skill listed with its input schema
2. It opens a Task and sends the search parameters (dates, origin, destination)
3. The flight agent moves the task to working, then to input-required when it needs the traveler to pick a fare class
4. The trip-planning agent relays that question to the end user, sends the answer back, and the task moves to completed with the booked itinerary

slides.title: A2A vs. MCP at a Glance

rows: A stateful Task with a lifecycle
Query a database, call an API
Delegate a sub-goal to a specialist agent

slides.title: When to Reach for A2A — and When Not To
bullets: Good fit: multi-vendor or multi-team systems where one agent needs to delegate real, open-ended work to another autonomous agent it doesn't control
Overkill: a single codebase calling its own internal functions — that's just a function call, not an agent negotiation
Never trust a signed Agent Card as a behavior guarantee — signing proves who published it, not that the agent is safe or competent
A2A and MCP are stackable: a single agent can be an MCP client for its tools and an A2A participant for peer agents, at the same time

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between MCP and A2A?
options: MCP is for text models, A2A is for image models
MCP connects an agent to tools and data; A2A connects one autonomous agent to another
They are competing standards for the same problem
A2A replaced MCP in 2026
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes how an agent calls tools, files, and data sources. A2A standardizes how one autonomous agent delegates work to another agent that has its own reasoning and goals. Most real systems use both together.

questions.prompt: What does an agent's Agent Card actually provide?
options: A log of every task the agent has ever completed
A published description of the agent's identity, skills, endpoint, and supported auth schemes
The agent's full source code
A billing invoice for API usage
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is a JSON document, published at a well-known URL, that lets a client discover what an agent can do and how to reach it — before any task is ever sent.

questions.prompt: Why does an A2A Task need an 'input-required' state instead of just completing or failing?
options: To save compute costs
Because many delegated tasks need a mid-task clarification or decision before they can finish
It's a required step for all tasks regardless of content
To signal that the transport layer (JSON-RPC vs. gRPC) is unsupported
questions.explanation: Real delegated work often can't be resolved in one shot — e.g. picking a fare class. 'input-required' lets the remote agent pause and ask, rather than forcing a binary completed/failed outcome.
